chapters.title: The Special Theory of Relativity
chapters.summary: This chapter introduces the special theory of relativity stemming from Einstein's two bold postulates, restricting discussion to inertial frames of reference. It shows how the entire theory is logically deduced from these postulates, beginning with the principle of relativity and the indistinguishability of inertial frames.
key_concepts: Constancy of the speed of light
Relativistic effects on space and time

book_skeleton.subject_overview: This text presents the special theory of relativity based on Einstein's two postulates, deriving its consequences through logical reasoning rather than appeals to everyday intuition. It focuses exclusively on inertial frames of reference and explores how the principle of relativity reshapes our understanding of space, time, and motion.

chapters.title: The Special Theory of Relativity
chapters.summary: This chapter introduces the special theory of relativity stemming from Einstein's two bold postulates, restricting discussion to inertial frames of reference. It shows how the entire theory is logically deduced from these postulates, beginning with the principle of relativity and the indistinguishability of inertial frames.

events.text: Inertial frame = steady velocity, no jerks
No experiment inside tells you if you are moving
No preferred frame: all motion is relative

events.title: Maxwell and the speed of light

events.text: Maxwell's laws look the same in every steady-moving frame, so light travels at speed c for everyone
A measures c. B also measures c.
Same speed for everyone means their clocks cannot agree
Q: B moves right at u = c/2; pulse W moves right at c relative to both A and B; at t=0 all at same place. Does AW = AB + BW?
B's diary: BA = AB and BW = AW at each t, so AW = BW while AB != 0
The expected relation AW = AB + BW fails; both A and B see W move at speed c, so simple distance addition breaks down.
Moving clock runs slow by the factor root of one minus v squared over c squared
Q: Train at 3e7 m/s; sleeps 10 p.m. to 4 a.m. on his watch. How long per station clocks?
Watch reading = proper time, delta t = 6 hours
Station clocks = improper time, delta t' = delta t / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)
delta t' = 6 hours 1.8 minutes
Q: Passenger is 6 ft in train frame, train moves at c/10. Height in ground frame?
L' = 5 feet 11.6 inches
Q: Rest length of box = 30 light seconds, train T1 speed = 0.8c. Find the time gap between D1 and D2 opening, in the frame of T1.
time gap = L * (v/c^2) * gamma
time elapsed = 40 seconds
Shrinks only along the motion
gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)
Q: Particle at rest at origin, constant force F from t=0. Find speed v at time t.
dp/dt = F
∫₀ᵖ dp = ∫₀ᵗ F dt  →  p = Ft
m₀v / √(1 − v²/c²) = Ft
v = Ftc / √(m₀²c² + F²t²),  v < c always
rest energy = m-naught c squared
Total energy = rest energy + kinetic energy

events.latex: E = \frac{m_0 c^2}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} = m_0 c^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_0 v^2 + \cdots

events.text: Q: A mass of 3.6 g is fully converted into energy. How many kilowatt hours are obtained?
1\ \text{kWh} = 10^3\ \text{J/s} \times 3600\ \text{s} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}
E = 9 \times 10^{7}\ \text{kWh}
photon: no rest mass, all energy
Nothing exceeds c, about 300000 kilometers per second
cause then effect, in my frame
Limit protects cause before effect
Earth sees outbound 10 years, return 10 years, total 20 years
Ram ages 12 years, Balram ages 20 years
Q: Earth-planet distance = 8 light-years; speed of S1 = 0.8c, speed of S2 = 0.8c. Ram travels out and back. How much do Ram and Balram each age?
Earth-frame time one way = 8 light-years / 0.8c = 10 years
Ship time one way = 10 years x 0.6 = 6 years
Ram total = 6 + 6 = 12 years; Balram total = 10 + 10 = 20 years
Ram ages 12 years, Balram ages 20 years - Ram is younger by 8 years
Q: From Ram's frame, how much younger does he conclude Balram is?
Contracted distance = 8 light-years × 0.6 = 4.8 light-years
Time per leg = 4.8 light-years ÷ 0.8c = 6 years
Total trip on Ram's clock = 6 + 6 = 12 years
Balram's clock = 12 years × 0.6 = 7.2 years
Ram concludes Balram is 12 − 7.2 = 4.8 years younger
Q: Contracted distance 4.8 light-years, planet approaches at 0.8c, reaching Ram in 6 years. Resolve the twin paradox.
Earth & planet clocks advance = 6 years × 0.6 = 3.6 years
In S1: planet clock leads by 6.4 years (planet at rear)
Leaving S1: earth clock = 3.6 years, planet clock = 6.4 + 3.6 = 10 years
Entering S2: earth clock leads by 6.4 years → earth reads 10 + 6.4 = 16.4 years
Earth clock = 16.4 + 3.6 = 20 years — paradox resolved.
only the traveller switches frames

chapters.narration_text:
<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_1>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_1:two_frames>> You are reading this while hurtling through space at thirty kilometers per second around the Sun. So why can you pour a glass of water without spilling a single drop? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:The Principle of Relativity|id=sec-1>> Here is the answer, and it is one of the deepest ideas in all of physics. Steady motion, motion with no jerks and no turning, simply cannot be felt from the inside. Picture yourself <<FOCUS:frame-platform>> standing on a railway platform. You drop a stone, and it <<TRACE:stone-platform>> lands neatly on your left foot. Now climb aboard a train that is <<FOCUS:frame-train+velocity-arrow>> gliding past at a steady one hundred twenty kilometers per hour, and let it slide along to the right. Drop the very same stone <<TRACE:stone-train>> inside that moving train. <<UNFOCUS>> Where does it land? <<FOCUS:stone-train+stone-platform>> Right on your left foot, exactly as before. <<UNFOCUS>> Nothing is different. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Inertial frame = steady velocity, no jerks|id=text-1>> A point of view from which you measure motion is <<FOCUS:frame-platform+frame-train>> called a frame of reference, and one moving at a steady velocity, with no acceleration, is called an inertial frame. <<UNFOCUS>> Now, here is the interesting thing. Could any experiment whatsoever, done sealed inside that train, reveal that you are moving? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:No experiment inside tells you if you are moving|id=key-1>> The answer is no. Not the stone, not a swinging pendulum, not a thrown ball. No experiment inside can ever tell you whether the train is parked at the platform or racing across the country. <<PAUSE:short>> The reason is that Newton's law keeps exactly the same form in every inertial frame: force always equals mass times acceleration, <<FOCUS:frame-platform+frame-train>> on the platform and on the train alike. <<UNFOCUS>> Since identical experiments are governed by identical laws, they must give identical results, no matter which frame you are sitting in. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:No preferred frame: all motion is relative|id=key-2>> So there is no special, preferred frame that nature calls truly at rest. Every smoothly moving frame is just as good as any other. <<PAUSE:short>> You may <<FOCUS:frame-platform>> call the platform at rest and the train moving, or <<FOCUS:frame-train>> the train at rest and the platform moving. <<UNFOCUS>> Both stories are equally true, because all motion at constant velocity is purely relative.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_2>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_2:two_observers_light_pulse>> Two friends start at the very same spot. One stays put, the other races off to the right at half the speed of light. They both watch the same flash of light fly away — and they both measure it pulling away at exactly the same speed. How can that possibly be true? <<SECTION:Maxwell and the speed of light|id=sec-1>> To see where this puzzle comes from, we need Maxwell's laws — the rules of electricity and magnetism. Buried inside them is a number: the speed of light through empty space, about three hundred million meters per second, which we call c. Maxwell's laws hide a fixed number for the speed of light: it depends only on two constants of empty space, and it comes out to about three hundred million meters per second. <<WRITE_EQUATION:c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}} \approx 3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now here is the big question. We already believe the laws of physics look the same to anyone moving at a steady speed — inside a smoothly gliding ship you cannot tell you are moving at all. So do Maxwell's laws look the same to everyone too? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Maxwell's laws look the same in every steady-moving frame, so light travels at speed c for everyone|id=key-1>> And the answer, confirmed by experiment, is yes. The very same Maxwell's laws hold for every observer moving at a constant speed. But that has a startling price: the speed of light, c, must come out the same for all of them. <<PAUSE:short>> Let me show you why that feels impossible. <<FOCUS:observer-a>> Here is observer A, standing still. At the very first instant, A, observer B, and a flash of light W <<FOCUS:observer-a+observer-b+light-pulse>> are all together at one spot. Now <<FOCUS:observer-b+velocity-b>> let B slide off to the right at half the speed of light, while <<FOCUS:light-pulse>> the flash races to the right at the full speed of light, leaving everyone behind. <<UNFOCUS>> Here is the everyday answer you would expect. Since B is chasing after the light, surely the light should <<FOCUS:speed-from-b>> pull away from B more slowly than it pulls away from <<FOCUS:speed-from-a>> the stationary A. <<UNFOCUS>> That is just common sense, like a fast car gaining on a slow one. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:A measures c. B also measures c.|id=text-1>> But nature refuses. <<FOCUS:speed-from-a>> A measures the light leaving at speed c — and B, even while chasing it at half c, <<FOCUS:speed-from-b>> also measures it leaving at the full speed c. <<UNFOCUS>> The same flash, the same speed, for both of them. <<WRITE_KEY:Same speed for everyone means their clocks cannot agree|id=key-2>> Sit with how strange that is. If A and B both started together, and both see the light always exactly the same distance ahead at every tick, then the simple idea that distances just add up must break. <<PAUSE:short>> So which piece of common sense has to give way? Something we never doubted must be quietly wrong. <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose <<FOCUS:velocity-b>> B moves away from A at speed u equals c over two, toward the right. A light pulse, call it W, <<FOCUS:light-pulse>> moves at speed c toward the right relative to both A and B. <<UNFOCUS>> And at time zero, A, B, and W are all at the same place. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: B moves right at u = c/2; pulse W moves right at c relative to both A and B; at t=0 all at same place. Does AW = AB + BW?|id=ex-q-1>> Each observer keeps a diary of distances over time. In A's diary: at one second AB is one point five times ten to the eighth meters and AW is three times ten to the eighth meters; at two seconds AB is three times ten to the eighth meters and AW is six times ten to the eighth meters; at three seconds AB is four point five times ten to the eighth meters and AW is nine times ten to the eighth meters. <<WRITE_STEP:A's diary: t=1s -> AB=1.5e8 m, AW=3e8 m; t=2s -> AB=3e8 m, AW=6e8 m; t=3s -> AB=4.5e8 m, AW=9e8 m|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now B's diary shows the same numbers: BA equals AB and BW equals AW at each time. So at every instant we find AW equals BW even though AB is not zero. <<WRITE_STEP:B's diary: BA = AB and BW = AW at each t, so AW = BW while AB != 0|id=ex-step-1-2>> But ordinary thinking says AW should equal AB plus BW. Here that relation simply does not hold, because both observers measure the pulse <<FOCUS:speed-from-a+speed-from-b>> moving away at the same speed c. <<UNFOCUS>> The two diaries suggest something is wrong with our everyday rule of adding distances. <<WRITE_ANSWER:The expected relation AW = AB + BW fails; both A and B see W move at speed c, so simple distance addition breaks down.|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> It is time itself. The only way everyone can agree on the speed of light is if they disagree on time — one second for A is simply not the same second for B. What feels like a single moment for one observer is not one moment for the other. <<PAUSE:short>> And that is the doorway into relativity. We held onto Maxwell's laws and the speed of light for every observer — and in return we had to give up the idea that time ticks the same for everyone. Next, we will see exactly how clocks and rulers must change to keep this promise. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_3>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_3:light_clock>> Build a clock out of nothing but a flash of light bouncing between two mirrors, <<FOCUS:mirror-bottom>> one on the bottom <<FOCUS:mirror-top>> and one on top. <<UNFOCUS>> Every round trip is one tick. <<SECTION:The light clock|id=sec-1>> Sitting still, the pulse just goes <<TRACE:light-vertical>> straight up to the top mirror and straight back down. Simple, honest, and the time for one tick <<FOCUS:leg-ct0>> we will call t-nought. <<UNFOCUS>> Now here is the interesting thing. Suppose I run past this clock, or what is the same, the clock <<FOCUS:base-vt>> glides past me to the right at speed v. <<UNFOCUS>> While the light travels from the bottom mirror up to the top, the whole clock has moved sideways. So from where I stand, the pulse does not go straight up. It goes along a <<TRACE:light-diagonal>> slanted, diagonal path. Look closely and you will see <<FOCUS:base-vt+hyp-ct+leg-ct0>> a right triangle hiding here. The bottom side is <<FOCUS:base-vt>> how far the clock moved, v times t. <<FOCUS:hyp-ct>> The slanted side is the path the light took, and <<FOCUS:leg-ct0>> the upright side is the same mirror gap as before. <<UNFOCUS>> Now the crucial fact that nature forces on us: the speed of light is the same for everyone. So that long diagonal path was also covered at speed c, which means <<FOCUS:hyp-ct>> the slanted side has length c times t. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here is the puzzle. The light in the moving clock had a longer road to travel, but it is forbidden from going any faster. So what has to give? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:hyp-ct>> The slanted light path squared equals <<FOCUS:base-vt>> the sideways distance squared plus <<FOCUS:leg-ct0>> the mirror gap squared, just Pythagoras on the triangle we drew. <<WRITE_EQUATION:(ct)^2 = (vt)^2 + (ct_0)^2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Moving clock runs slow by the factor root of one minus v squared over c squared|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Time itself must stretch. Pythagoras on this triangle gives c times t for the slanted side, squared, equals v times t squared plus c times t-nought squared, and out pops the factor square root of one minus v squared over c squared. The moving clock ticks slower. <<PAUSE:short>> Solving that triangle for the time tells us the moving clock's tick is the resting tick divided by the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:t = \dfrac{t_0}{\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}}}|id=eq-2|boxed>> Say it plainly, because it is strange: a moving clock runs slow, by exactly that square root of one minus v squared over c squared. And it is not a trick of this clock. Every clock, even your heartbeat, must agree. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_3:length_contraction>> <<SECTION:Length contraction|id=sec-2>> Now if time gets squeezed, something else must give too. Picture a measuring rod <<FOCUS:rod-rest>> lying still in its own frame, at its <<FOCUS:rest-length-label>> full, honest length L-nought. When that same rod <<FOCUS:rod-moving>> flies past you along its own length, to keep the speed of light coming out the same for everyone, <<FOCUS:moving-dim-arrow>> the rod must appear shorter, shrunk by that very same factor. <<PAUSE:short>> The moving rod's length is <<FOCUS:length-label>> its rest length multiplied by that same square root of one minus v squared over c squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:L = L_0\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}}|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. A person on a train moving at three times ten to the seventh meters per second goes to sleep at ten p.m. by his watch and gets up at four a.m. That's six hours of sleep on his watch. The question is: how long did he sleep according to the clocks at the stations? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Train at 3e7 m/s; sleeps 10 p.m. to 4 a.m. on his watch. How long per station clocks?|id=ex-q-1>> First, let's identify which time is which. Both events, falling asleep and waking up, are recorded by the single watch he carries, so the watch reading is the proper time interval. That proper time is six hours. <<WRITE_STEP:Watch reading = proper time, delta t = 6 hours|id=ex-step-1-1>> The station clocks belong to the ground frame, and in that frame he falls asleep at one place and wakes up at another. So the station clocks give the improper time interval, which is longer. We get it by multiplying by the gamma factor: delta t prime equals gamma times delta t, which is delta t over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Station clocks = improper time, delta t' = delta t / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we put in the numbers. The speed v is three times ten to the seventh meters per second, and the speed of light c is three times ten to the eighth meters per second. So v over c is one tenth. Squaring that gives one hundredth, and one minus one hundredth leaves ninety-nine hundredths under the root. <<WRITE_STEP:v/c = 1/10, so delta t' = 6 h / sqrt(1 - 1/100) = 6 h * sqrt(100/99)|id=ex-step-1-3>> The gamma factor is therefore the square root of one hundred over ninety-nine. Multiplying six hours by that factor, the sleep duration in the ground frame comes out to six hours and one point eight minutes. <<WRITE_ANSWER:delta t' = 6 hours 1.8 minutes|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A passenger lies in a train with his head toward the engine and feet toward the guard's coach, so his body is measured parallel to the direction of motion. In the train frame he measures six feet tall, and the train moves past the ground at a speed of c divided by ten. The question is: how tall does he appear in the ground frame? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Passenger is 6 ft in train frame, train moves at c/10. Height in ground frame?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by noting that the six feet is the rest length, since the passenger is at rest in the train. In the ground frame he is moving, so his length parallel to the motion is contracted. Here v over c is one tenth, so the contraction factor is the square root of one minus one tenth squared, which is the square root of ninety-nine over one hundred. <<WRITE_STEP:L' = 6 ft × \u221a(1 - (1/10)\u00b2) = 6 ft × \u221a(99/100)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Multiplying six feet by the square root of ninety-nine over one hundred, the answer is five feet eleven point six inches. <<WRITE_ANSWER:L' = 5 feet 11.6 inches|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose the rest length of the box is thirty light seconds, and the train T one travels at a speed of zero point eight c. We want to find the time elapsed between the opening of door one and door two in the frame of T one. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Rest length of box = 30 light seconds, train T1 speed = 0.8c. Find the time gap between D1 and D2 opening, in the frame of T1.|id=ex-q-1>> In the frame of T one, the box moves with a speed of zero point eight c, so v over c is zero point eight. That gives us a gamma factor of one divided by the square root of one minus zero point eight squared, which works out to one divided by zero point six. <<WRITE_STEP:v/c = 0.8, so gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - 0.8^2) = 1 / 0.6|id=ex-step-1-1>> In this frame, door two opens after door one. The time elapsed between the openings is given by the formula L times v over c squared, times gamma. <<WRITE_STEP:time gap = L * (v/c^2) * gamma|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we substitute. L is thirty light seconds, which we can write as thirty seconds times c. Then we plug in v as zero point eight c, and gamma as one over zero point six. So we get thirty seconds times c, times zero point eight c, all divided by c squared times zero point six. <<WRITE_STEP:= (30 light seconds * 0.8c) / (c^2 * 0.6) = (30 s)c * 0.8c / (c^2 * 0.6)|id=ex-step-1-3>> The c squared cancels top and bottom, leaving thirty times zero point eight divided by zero point six seconds. And the answer is forty seconds. <<WRITE_ANSWER:time elapsed = 40 seconds|id=ex-ans-1>> And notice, it <<FOCUS:rod-moving+velocity>> only shrinks along the direction it moves. <<FOCUS:rod-rest>> Across its motion, nothing changes. <<WRITE_TEXT:Shrinks only along the motion|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> That sideways agreement is exactly what the relativity principle demands. So both clocks and rods were honest tools, yet motion bends what they read. Moving clocks run slow, moving rods grow short, and the same little factor, square root of one minus v squared over c squared, governs both. We never notice it because v is tiny compared with c. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_4>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_4:gamma_runaway>> Push a particle with a steady force forever, and Newton promises it just keeps speeding up, faster and faster, with <<TRACE:newton-line>> no ceiling at all. But nature has <<FOCUS:light-wall>> hung a wall in the sky, the speed of light, and nothing made of matter ever gets through it. <<SECTION:Dynamics at large velocity|id=sec-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> So something in the old rule must bend. The rule we are bending is the one you have trusted for years, force equals mass times acceleration. Here is the honest question. If a constant force never stops pushing, why does the particle refuse to break the light barrier? Where does all that pushing go? <<PAUSE:long>> The secret is momentum. In Newton's world momentum is simply mass times velocity, so push harder and it grows without limit, <<TRACE:newton-line>> a perfectly straight line climbing forever. <<WRITE_TEXT:gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)|id=text-gamma>> <<UNFOCUS>> But relativity inserts a new character into the formula, a number we call gamma, equal to one over the square root of one minus the velocity squared over the speed of light squared. <<PAUSE:short>> Relativity inserts a number gamma equal to one over the square root of one minus the velocity squared over the speed of light squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now here is the lovely part. At everyday speeds, walking, driving, even rocketing into orbit, v over c is so tiny that gamma is almost exactly one, so <<FOCUS:relativity-curve+newton-line>> the relativistic curve lies right on top of Newton's line. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> That overlap is why Newton's law has worked flawlessly for three centuries. In <<FOCUS:agreement-region>> this whole shaded region the two pictures simply agree. <<UNFOCUS>> So the real momentum of a particle is its rest mass times gamma times its velocity. The rest mass is just the ordinary mass you would measure standing still beside it. <<PAUSE:short>> The real momentum of a particle is its rest mass times gamma times its velocity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{p} = m_0\,\gamma\,\vec{v}|id=eq-2|boxed>> And watch what gamma does as <<TRACE:relativity-curve>> the speed creeps toward the speed of light. The bottom of that fraction, the square root, shrinks toward zero, so gamma swells toward infinity, and the momentum shoots straight up. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So now we can answer where the pushing goes. The force keeps adding momentum, but because gamma is exploding, almost all of that momentum goes into making the particle harder to accelerate, not faster. Here's an example from the chapter. A particle starts at rest at the origin, and a constant force F begins acting on it at time t equals zero. Because the particle starts from rest and the force always points the same way, the motion is along one direction only. We want the speed of the particle at time t. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Particle at rest at origin, constant force F from t=0. Find speed v at time t.|id=ex-q-1>> We start from the equation of motion, which says the rate of change of momentum equals F. That is, d p by d t equals F. <<WRITE_STEP:dp/dt = F|id=ex-step-1-1>> The law of motion says force equals the rate of change of this relativistic momentum. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt}|id=eq-3|boxed>> Now we integrate both sides. The integral of d p from zero to p equals the integral of F d t from zero to t. Since F is constant, this gives p equals F times t. <<WRITE_STEP:∫₀ᵖ dp = ∫₀ᵗ F dt  →  p = Ft|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we put in the relativistic momentum: p equals m naught times v divided by the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. Setting that equal to F times t gives m naught v over square root of one minus v squared over c squared equals F times t. <<WRITE_STEP:m₀v / √(1 − v²/c²) = Ft|id=ex-step-1-3>> Solving this for v, we find v equals F times t times c divided by the square root of m naught squared c squared plus F squared t squared. Notice that however large t may be, v can never exceed c. No matter how long you apply the force, the speed stays less than the speed of light. <<WRITE_ANSWER:v = Ftc / √(m₀²c² + F²t²),  v < c always|id=ex-ans-1>> <<WRITE_KEY:p = m0 * gamma * v -> infinite inertia as v -> c|id=key-momentum>>That growing gamma acts like a growing inertia. Near the speed of light the particle behaves as if its mass is enormous, so no finite force can ever <<FOCUS:light-wall>> shove it across the wall. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> And the law of motion itself is gentler than you might fear. We simply say force equals the rate of change of this relativistic momentum, and if no force acts, that momentum stays perfectly constant, just like before.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_5>>
There is a furnace inside the pencil on your desk; if you could unlock the energy hiding in just one gram of it, you could power a small town for days. <<SECTION:Mass is energy|id=sec-1>> The reason is one of the strangest discoveries in all of physics: mass and energy are not two different things, they are two names for exactly the same thing. <<PAUSE:short>> Einstein found that any lump of mass already holds an enormous store of energy, just by existing, and the amount is the mass multiplied by the speed of light squared. <<PAUSE:short>> And here is why the number is so huge: the speed of light is three hundred million meters per second, so squaring it gives a colossal factor, which is why a speck of matter hides a town-sized furnace. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_5:mass_energy_ledger>> Now let me show you where this energy lives, because a particle has <<FOCUS:rest-energy-segment+kinetic-energy-segment>> two kinds of it stacked together. <<WRITE_TEXT:rest energy = m-naught c squared|id=text-rest>> Even a particle sitting perfectly still, doing nothing, owns <<FOCUS:rest-energy-segment>> this left chunk: its rest energy, the mass it has at rest times the speed of light squared. <<UNFOCUS>> A particle at rest still holds energy equal to its rest mass times the speed of light squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:E_0 = m_0 c^2|id=eq-1|boxed>> But watch what happens <<FOCUS:push-arrow>> when I push it; I do work on it, and that work has to go somewhere. <<UNFOCUS>> So here is the puzzle: if I keep pushing a particle to make it faster and faster, the energy I pour in keeps growing without limit, but energy is mass, so what happens to the mass? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The mass actually grows; the faster it moves, the heavier it gets, because the extra energy I gave it shows up as extra mass, which is exactly <<FOCUS:kinetic-energy-segment>> this growing right-hand chunk. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Total energy = rest energy + kinetic energy|id=key-split>> So <<FOCUS:total-energy-bar>> the whole bar is the total energy: the rest energy it always had, plus the kinetic energy of its motion. <<PAUSE:short>> And the beautiful part: when the speed is small compared to light, this extra kinetic chunk shrinks down to exactly the <<FOCUS:kinetic-seg-math>> one-half m v squared you already learned, so relativity contains your old physics inside it. <<UNFOCUS>> The total energy is the rest energy plus, for small speeds, the familiar one-half mass times velocity squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:E = \frac{m_0 c^2}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} = m_0 c^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_0 v^2 + \cdots|id=eq-2|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose a mass of three point six grams, that is three point six times ten to the minus three kilograms, is fully converted into energy. The question asks: how many kilowatt hours of electrical energy will we obtain? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A mass of 3.6 g is fully converted into energy. How many kilowatt hours are obtained?|id=ex-q-1>> Energy and momentum lock together, and for light with no rest mass this leaves energy equal to momentum times the speed of light. <<WRITE_EQUATION:E^2 = m_0^2 c^4 + p^2 c^2|id=eq-3|boxed>> We start from Einstein's relation, <<FOCUS:total-label>> energy equals m times c squared, where c is the speed of light, three times ten to the eighth meters per second. <<WRITE_EQUATION:E = mc^2|id=ex-eq-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now we substitute the numbers. We put in three point six times ten to the minus three kilograms for the mass, and three times ten to the eighth meters per second for c, then square that speed. <<WRITE_STEP:E = (3.6 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{kg})(3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s})^2|id=ex-step-1-1>> Multiplying everything out, the energy comes to thirty-two point four times ten to the thirteenth joules. <<WRITE_STEP:E = 32.4 \times 10^{13}\ \text{J}|id=ex-step-1-2>> To convert to kilowatt hours, recall that one kilowatt hour equals ten to the third joules per second times three thousand six hundred seconds, which is three point six times ten to the sixth joules. So we divide our energy by that. <<WRITE_STEP:1\ \text{kWh} = 10^3\ \text{J/s} \times 3600\ \text{s} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}|id=ex-step-1-3>> Dividing thirty-two point four times ten to the thirteenth joules by three point six times ten to the sixth joules, the answer is nine times ten to the seventh kilowatt hours. <<WRITE_ANSWER:E = 9 \times 10^{7}\ \text{kWh}|id=ex-ans-1>> <<WRITE_TEXT:photon: no rest mass, all energy|id=text-photon>> One last wonder: a particle of light has no rest mass at all, so <<FOCUS:rest-energy-segment>> its left chunk vanishes; it is pure energy and pure momentum, with energy equal to its momentum times the speed of light. <<UNFOCUS>> Remember this: mass and energy are one single thing, and the rule that ties everything together is energy equals m times c squared. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_6>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_6:cause_effect_frames>> Picture a frame where a bullet smashes into the bird before the trigger is even pulled, or a dog dies before it is ever born. That is the absurd world we have to rule out. Here is where it comes from. Earlier we kept pushing on a particle, expecting it to go faster and faster forever, but its speed crept toward one wall and never crossed it: the speed of light, c, about three hundred thousand kilometers per second. <<SECTION:The cosmic speed limit|id=sec-1>> <<WRITE_KEY:Nothing exceeds c, about 300000 kilometers per second|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Any speed v of a particle or signal must stay below the speed of light c, which is about three hundred million meters per second. <<WRITE_EQUATION:v < c \approx 3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now you might ask: why should nature care so fiercely about this one number? Why not just let something, anything, go a little bit faster? <<PAUSE:long>> The answer is about cause and effect. Let me set up two observers. <<FOCUS:frame-rest>> Here is me, at rest, with <<FOCUS:frame-rest-space>> space across and <<FOCUS:frame-rest-time>> time going up. And here is a friend <<FOCUS:frame-moving+velocity-arrow>> gliding past to the right at a steady speed v. <<UNFOCUS>> Relativity insists the laws of physics look exactly the same for both of us. Now suppose I fire off a signal that beats light to its target. <<FOCUS:cause-event>> The cause is here, <<FOCUS:effect-event>> the effect is over there, and <<TRACE:faster-than-light-signal>> the line between them is almost flat because the signal is so fast. <<WRITE_TEXT:cause then effect, in my frame|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> In my frame, fine: cause first, then effect. But watch what my moving friend sees, because in relativity <<FOCUS:frame-moving-time+frame-moving>> space and time tilt together when you change frames. <<PAUSE:short>> For a signal faster than light, that tilt is enough to flip the order: my friend sees <<FOCUS:effect-event+cause-event>> the effect happen before the cause. <<UNFOCUS>> The bird is hit before the trigger moves. That is the impossible world. So the speed limit is not a stubborn rule about how engines work. It is nature protecting cause and effect: if effect can never come before its cause in any frame, then c must be <<FOCUS:light-cone-line>> the ultimate speed. <<WRITE_KEY:Limit protects cause before effect|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> And this is bigger than bullets and birds. No particle, no message, no influence of any kind can outrun light, because all of them would break this same chain of cause and effect. <<PAUSE:short>> Now here is a delicious loophole. Physicists asked: what about particles that are born already faster than light and can never slow below it? They called them tachyons. In their hypothetical world effect always precedes cause, and crucially they could never interact with us, so our cause and effect stays safe. Whether tachyons truly exist is still an open question. So remember this: light's speed, about three hundred thousand kilometers per second, is the universe's ultimate speed limit, and nature enforces it not out of stubbornness but to keep every cause safely ahead of its effect. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_7>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_7:twin_journey>> Two twins, the same age. One blasts off to a far planet and races back, and when he steps out of the ship he is younger than his brother. Not a trick, not a feeling, genuinely younger. <<SECTION:The set-up|id=sec-1>> <<FOCUS:earth>> Here is Earth, and <<FOCUS:planet>> way over here is a distant planet sitting still, eight light-years away. <<FOCUS:balram-clock>> Balram stays home; <<FOCUS:ram-clock>> Ram takes the trip. Ram <<TRACE:outbound-path>> rides one ship out at eight tenths the speed of light, and at the planet he leaps onto a <<TRACE:return-path>> second ship heading straight back, again at eight tenths the speed of light. <<UNFOCUS>> Now here is the strange thing we learned earlier: when something moves that fast, its clocks run slow. <<FOCUS:ram-clock>> Ram's watch, his heartbeat, even his breathing, all slow down. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The amount a moving clock slows down is captured by one number, called the time-dilation factor, gamma. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> How slow? We package the slowdown into one number called gamma, the time-dilation factor. At eight tenths of light speed it works out to exactly six tenths. Let's count from Balram's chair on Earth. For him, the planet is eight light-years away and Ram crawls there at eight tenths light speed, so <<FOCUS:outbound-path>> the trip out takes ten years. <<PAUSE:long>> <<WRITE_STEP:Earth sees outbound 10 years, return 10 years, total 20 years|id=step-1>> The return is <<FOCUS:return-path>> another ten years. So <<FOCUS:balram-clock>> Balram waits twenty whole years for his brother to come home. <<UNFOCUS>> The time that passes for the travelling twin equals the time on Earth multiplied by the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:t_{\text{Ram}} = t_{\text{Balram}} \times \sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> But Ram's clock ran slow the entire flight. Multiply Balram's twenty years by six tenths, and <<FOCUS:ram-clock>> only twelve years passed for Ram. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Ram ages 12 years, Balram ages 20 years|id=key-1>> So when Ram climbs out, <<FOCUS:ram-clock+balram-clock>> he has aged twelve years while Balram has aged twenty. <<UNFOCUS>> Ram really is eight years younger. <<SECTION:Where is the paradox?|id=sec-2>> Now, you should be itching to object. Motion is relative! From Ram's seat, it is Balram and the whole Earth that flew away and came back. Shouldn't Balram be the younger one? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here is the resolution. Look at the trip: <<FOCUS:turnaround>> only Ram turns around at the planet. <<UNFOCUS>> He jumps ships, he reverses, he switches from one moving frame to another. <<FOCUS:earth>> Balram never does anything but sit still. <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter, the twin paradox worked out with simple numbers. The distance between the earth and the planet is <<FOCUS:earth+planet>> eight light-years, measured in the earth frame. <<UNFOCUS>> Ram's outgoing spaceship S one moves at zero point eight c, and his return spaceship S two also moves at zero point eight c. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Earth-planet distance = 8 light-years; speed of S1 = 0.8c, speed of S2 = 0.8c. Ram travels out and back. How much do Ram and Balram each age?|id=ex-q-1>> Let's analyse everything from the point of view of Balram, who stays on the earth. For him both spaceships move at zero point eight c, so the time-dilation factor gamma is one over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared, which works out to one over zero point six. <<WRITE_STEP:gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = 1 / 0.6|id=ex-step-1-1>> Balram first calculates how long the outward trip takes in his own earth frame. That's the distance, eight light-years, divided by the speed, zero point eight c, which <<FOCUS:outbound-path>> gives ten years. <<WRITE_STEP:Earth-frame time one way = 8 light-years / 0.8c = 10 years|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> But during all those ten years, time runs slowly on the moving spaceship S one. The ship's clocks read only ten years times zero point six, which is <<FOCUS:ram-clock>> six years for the outbound leg. <<WRITE_STEP:Ship time one way = 10 years x 0.6 = 6 years|id=ex-step-1-3>> Then Ram <<FOCUS:turnaround>> jumps into S two for the return journey. <<UNFOCUS>> Again ten years pass on the earth, but on the spaceship that leg is clocked at only six years. So <<FOCUS:ram-clock+balram-clock>> Ram's total is six plus six, twelve years, while Balram lives through ten plus ten, twenty years. <<WRITE_STEP:Ram total = 6 + 6 = 12 years; Balram total = 10 + 10 = 20 years|id=ex-step-1-4>> <<UNFOCUS>> And so the answer is that Ram has aged only twelve years while Balram has aged twenty years, making Ram younger than Balram by eight years. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Ram ages 12 years, Balram ages 20 years - Ram is younger by 8 years|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter on the twin paradox. Let's analyze the journey from the traveling twin Ram's point of view. From Ram's frame, <<FOCUS:earth+planet>> the distance between earth and the planet is not the full eight light-years that Balram measures. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: From Ram's frame, how much younger does he conclude Balram is?|id=ex-q-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> We start by contracting the distance. To Ram, <<FOCUS:outbound-path>> the separation shrinks by a factor of zero point six, so the contracted distance is eight light-years times zero point six, which equals four point eight light-years. <<WRITE_STEP:Contracted distance = 8 light-years × 0.6 = 4.8 light-years|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now, <<FOCUS:planet>> the planet is approaching Ram at zero point eight c. So the time taken for the planet to reach him is four point eight light-years divided by zero point eight c, which <<FOCUS:ram-clock>> gives six years for that leg. <<WRITE_STEP:Time per leg = 4.8 light-years ÷ 0.8c = 6 years|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> On the return leg, the earth is again four point eight light-years away approaching at zero point eight c, taking another six years. So according to Ram's clock, <<FOCUS:ram-clock>> his total trip was twelve years. <<WRITE_STEP:Total trip on Ram's clock = 6 + 6 = 12 years|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's where the paradox bites. As twelve years pass on Ram's clock, he calculates that <<FOCUS:balram-clock>> Balram's clock advanced only twelve years times zero point six, which is seven point two years. <<WRITE_STEP:Balram's clock = 12 years × 0.6 = 7.2 years|id=ex-step-1-4>> <<UNFOCUS>> So from Ram's analysis, Balram should be twelve minus seven point two, which is four point eight years younger than him. Each twin thinks the other is younger, and that is the paradox. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Ram concludes Balram is 12 − 7.2 = 4.8 years younger|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter that resolves the twin paradox. The captain tells Ram: <<FOCUS:planet>> planet P is four point eight light-years away, contracted in our frame, and it's coming towards us at zero point eight c, so it will take six years on his clock for the planet to reach us. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Contracted distance 4.8 light-years, planet approaches at 0.8c, reaching Ram in 6 years. Resolve the twin paradox.|id=ex-q-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Ram works out the first piece. The clocks on the earth and on the planet will advance by six years times zero point six, which is three point six years, by the time the planet reaches us. <<WRITE_STEP:Earth & planet clocks advance = 6 years × 0.6 = 3.6 years|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now the captain explains the synchronization. In Ram's frame S one, <<FOCUS:planet>> the planet's clock is at the rear end, so it's running six point four years ahead of the earth's clock. <<UNFOCUS>> When the earth's clock read zero, the planet's clock already read six point four years. <<WRITE_STEP:In S1: planet clock leads by 6.4 years (planet at rear)|id=ex-step-1-2>> As the planet reaches us, both clocks advance by those three point six years. So when you jump out of frame S one, <<FOCUS:balram-clock>> the earth's clock reads three point six years, but <<FOCUS:planet>> the planet's clock reads ten years. <<WRITE_STEP:Leaving S1: earth clock = 3.6 years, planet clock = 6.4 + 3.6 = 10 years|id=ex-step-1-3>> Now you <<FOCUS:turnaround>> board frame S two, and the commander explains the flip. <<UNFOCUS>> In this frame it is the earth's clock that leads by six point four years. The planet's clock reads ten years, so the earth's clock must read sixteen point four years. <<WRITE_STEP:Entering S2: earth clock leads by 6.4 years → earth reads 10 + 6.4 = 16.4 years|id=ex-step-1-4>> During the six years you spend on S two heading back, the earth's clock advances another three point six years, <<FOCUS:balram-clock>> reaching twenty years. <<UNFOCUS>> The traveler aged less, and the paradox is resolved. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Earth clock = 16.4 + 3.6 = 20 years — paradox resolved.|id=ex-ans-1>> <<WRITE_TEXT:only the traveller switches frames|id=text-1>> <<FOCUS:turnaround>> That turnaround makes the twins genuinely different. <<UNFOCUS>> They are not interchangeable, so there is no contradiction, only an honest answer. <<PAUSE:short>> So the rule stands: the moving clock runs slow, and because <<FOCUS:turnaround>> only Ram did the travelling and the turning, Ram is the one who comes home young. <<PAUSE:short>>

lecture_plan.chapter_arc: Starting from two deceptively simple postulates — that the laws of physics look the same in every inertial frame, and that light always travels at c — we follow the chain of logic to its astonishing conclusions. We discover that space and time themselves bend to keep light's speed constant, that motion reshapes mass and energy, and that these are not mathematical tricks but the real architecture of the universe.
lecture_plan.opening_hook: Drop a stone on a smoothly moving train and it lands on your foot just as it would on the platform — so how do you ever know you're moving? Einstein took that innocent fact, added one stubborn truth about light, and rebuilt our entire picture of space and time.

coverage_checklist.description: State Einstein's two postulates and explain why no experiment can detect uniform motion (the principle of relativity)
Show that requiring Maxwell's laws to hold in all inertial frames forces the speed of light to be the same for everyone
Derive and connect time dilation and length contraction to everyday-relatable thought experiments (moving rods and clocks)
Show how Newton's second law is corrected at high speed and how mass grows with velocity
Explain mass-energy equivalence (E = mc^2) and its enormous numerical significance
Explain why c is the ultimate speed limit, tying it back to the growth of mass under continued force
Resolve the twin paradox, showing time dilation is real and that the asymmetry comes from acceleration

lecture_plan.closing_summary: We began with a stone dropped on a moving train and the puzzle of how you'd ever know you were moving at all. From that simple principle of relativity, plus the insistence that light always travels at c, everything else followed by pure logic: moving clocks run slow, moving rulers shrink, mass grows with speed, no object can ever reach the speed of light, and a sliver of mass hides a colossal store of energy in E = mc squared. The twin paradox showed us these effects are not illusions but the genuine fabric of reality. The deepest lesson is that two innocent-looking postulates, taken seriously, were enough to remake space, time, mass, and energy — that's the power of demanding the laws of nature look the same for everyone.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_1:two_frames>> You are reading this while hurtling through space at thirty kilometers per second around the Sun. So why can you pour a glass of water without spilling a single drop? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:The Principle of Relativity|id=sec-1>> Here is the answer, and it is one of the deepest ideas in all of physics. Steady motion, motion with no jerks and no turning, simply cannot be felt from the inside. Picture yourself <<FOCUS:frame-platform>> standing on a railway platform. You drop a stone, and it <<TRACE:stone-platform>> lands neatly on your left foot. Now climb aboard a train that is <<FOCUS:frame-train+velocity-arrow>> gliding past at a steady one hundred twenty kilometers per hour, and let it slide along to the right. Drop the very same stone <<TRACE:stone-train>> inside that moving train. <<UNFOCUS>> Where does it land? <<FOCUS:stone-train+stone-platform>> Right on your left foot, exactly as before. <<UNFOCUS>> Nothing is different. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Inertial frame = steady velocity, no jerks|id=text-1>> A point of view from which you measure motion is <<FOCUS:frame-platform+frame-train>> called a frame of reference, and one moving at a steady velocity, with no acceleration, is called an inertial frame. <<UNFOCUS>> Now, here is the interesting thing. Could any experiment whatsoever, done sealed inside that train, reveal that you are moving? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:No experiment inside tells you if you are moving|id=key-1>> The answer is no. Not the stone, not a swinging pendulum, not a thrown ball. No experiment inside can ever tell you whether the train is parked at the platform or racing across the country. <<PAUSE:short>> The reason is that Newton's law keeps exactly the same form in every inertial frame: force always equals mass times acceleration, <<FOCUS:frame-platform+frame-train>> on the platform and on the train alike. <<UNFOCUS>> Since identical experiments are governed by identical laws, they must give identical results, no matter which frame you are sitting in. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:No preferred frame: all motion is relative|id=key-2>> So there is no special, preferred frame that nature calls truly at rest. Every smoothly moving frame is just as good as any other. <<PAUSE:short>> You may <<FOCUS:frame-platform>> call the platform at rest and the train moving, or <<FOCUS:frame-train>> the train at rest and the platform moving. <<UNFOCUS>> Both stories are equally true, because all motion at constant velocity is purely relative.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_2:two_observers_light_pulse>> Two friends start at the very same spot. One stays put, the other races off to the right at half the speed of light. They both watch the same flash of light fly away — and they both measure it pulling away at exactly the same speed. How can that possibly be true? <<SECTION:Maxwell and the speed of light|id=sec-1>> To see where this puzzle comes from, we need Maxwell's laws — the rules of electricity and magnetism. B also measures c.|id=text-1>> But nature refuses. <<FOCUS:speed-from-a>> A measures the light leaving at speed c — and B, even while chasing it at half c, <<FOCUS:speed-from-b>> also measures it leaving at the full speed c. <<UNFOCUS>> The same flash, the same speed, for both of them. <<WRITE_KEY:Same speed for everyone means their clocks cannot agree|id=key-2>> Sit with how strange that is. Something we never doubted must be quietly wrong. <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose <<FOCUS:velocity-b>> B moves away from A at speed u equals c over two, toward the right. In A's diary: at one second AB is one point five times ten to the eighth meters and AW is three times ten to the eighth meters; at two seconds AB is three times ten to the eighth meters and AW is six times ten to the eighth meters; at three seconds AB is four point five times ten to the eighth meters and AW is nine times ten to the eighth meters. <<WRITE_STEP:A's diary: t=1s -> AB=1.5e8 m, AW=3e8 m; t=2s -> AB=3e8 m, AW=6e8 m; t=3s -> AB=4.5e8 m, AW=9e8 m|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now B's diary shows the same numbers: BA equals AB and BW equals AW at each time. segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_3:light_clock>> Build a clock out of nothing but a flash of light bouncing between two mirrors, <<FOCUS:mirror-bottom>> one on the bottom <<FOCUS:mirror-top>> and one on top. <<UNFOCUS>> Every round trip is one tick. <<SECTION:The light clock|id=sec-1>> Sitting still, the pulse just goes <<TRACE:light-vertical>> straight up to the top mirror and straight back down. Simple, honest, and the time for one tick <<FOCUS:leg-ct0>> we will call t-nought. <<UNFOCUS>> Now here is the interesting thing. Suppose I run past this clock, or what is the same, the clock <<FOCUS:base-vt>> glides past me to the right at speed v. <<UNFOCUS>> While the light travels from the bottom mirror up to the top, the whole clock has moved sideways. So from where I stand, the pulse does not go straight up. It goes along a <<TRACE:light-diagonal>> slanted, diagonal path. Look closely and you will see <<FOCUS:base-vt+hyp-ct+leg-ct0>> a right triangle hiding here. The bottom side is <<FOCUS:base-vt>> how far the clock moved, v times t. <<FOCUS:hyp-ct>> The slanted side is the path the light took, and <<FOCUS:leg-ct0>> the upright side is the same mirror gap as before. <<UNFOCUS>> Now the crucial fact that nature forces on us: the speed of light is the same for everyone. So that long diagonal path was also covered at speed c, which means <<FOCUS:hyp-ct>> the slanted side has length c times t. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here is the puzzle. The light in the moving clock had a longer road to travel, but it is forbidden from going any faster. So what has to give? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:hyp-ct>> The slanted light path squared equals <<FOCUS:base-vt>> the sideways distance squared plus <<FOCUS:leg-ct0>> the mirror gap squared, just Pythagoras on the triangle we drew. <<WRITE_EQUATION:(ct)^2 = (vt)^2 + (ct_0)^2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Moving clock runs slow by the factor root of one minus v squared over c squared|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Time itself must stretch. Pythagoras on this triangle gives c times t for the slanted side, squared, equals v times t squared plus c times t-nought squared, and out pops the factor square root of one minus v squared over c squared. The moving clock ticks slower. <<PAUSE:short>> Solving that triangle for the time tells us the moving clock's tick is the resting tick divided by the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:t = \dfrac{t_0}{\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}}}|id=eq-2|boxed>> Say it plainly, because it is strange: a moving clock runs slow, by exactly that square root of one minus v squared over c squared. And it is not a trick of this clock. Every clock, even your heartbeat, must agree. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_3:length_contraction>> <<SECTION:Length contraction|id=sec-2>> Now if time gets squeezed, something else must give too. Picture a measuring rod <<FOCUS:rod-rest>> lying still in its own frame, at its <<FOCUS:rest-length-label>> full, honest length L-nought. When that same rod <<FOCUS:rod-moving>> flies past you along its own length, to keep the speed of light coming out the same for everyone, <<FOCUS:moving-dim-arrow>> the rod must appear shorter, shrunk by that very same factor. <<PAUSE:short>> The moving rod's length is <<FOCUS:length-label>> its rest length multiplied by that same square root of one minus v squared over c squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:L = L_0\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}}|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. A person on a train moving at three times ten to the seventh meters per second goes to sleep at ten p.m. by his watch and gets up at four a.m. That's six hours of sleep on his watch. The question is: how long did he sleep according to the clocks at the stations? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Train at 3e7 m/s; sleeps 10 p.m. to 4 a.m. on his watch. How long per station clocks?|id=ex-q-1>> First, let's identify which time is which. Both events, falling asleep and waking up, are recorded by the single watch he carries, so the watch reading is the proper time interval. That proper time is six hours. <<WRITE_STEP:Watch reading = proper time, delta t = 6 hours|id=ex-step-1-1>> The station clocks belong to the ground frame, and in that frame he falls asleep at one place and wakes up at another. So the station clocks give the improper time interval, which is longer. We get it by multiplying by the gamma factor: delta t prime equals gamma times delta t, which is delta t over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Station clocks = improper time, delta t' = delta t / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we put in the numbers. The speed v is three times ten to the seventh meters per second, and the speed of light c is three times ten to the eighth meters per second. So v over c is one tenth. Squaring that gives one hundredth, and one minus one hundredth leaves ninety-nine hundredths under the root. <<WRITE_STEP:v/c = 1/10, so delta t' = 6 h / sqrt(1 - 1/100) = 6 h * sqrt(100/99)|id=ex-step-1-3>> The gamma factor is therefore the square root of one hundred over ninety-nine. Multiplying six hours by that factor, the sleep duration in the ground frame comes out to six hours and one point eight minutes. <<WRITE_ANSWER:delta t' = 6 hours 1.8 minutes|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A passenger lies in a train with his head toward the engine and feet toward the guard's coach, so his body is measured parallel to the direction of motion. In the train frame he measures six feet tall, and the train moves past the ground at a speed of c divided by ten. The question is: how tall does he appear in the ground frame? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Passenger is 6 ft in train frame, train moves at c/10. Height in ground frame?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by noting that the six feet is the rest length, since the passenger is at rest in the train. In the ground frame he is moving, so his length parallel to the motion is contracted. Here v over c is one tenth, so the contraction factor is the square root of one minus one tenth squared, which is the square root of ninety-nine over one hundred. <<WRITE_STEP:L' = 6 ft × \u221a(1 - (1/10)\u00b2) = 6 ft × \u221a(99/100)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Multiplying six feet by the square root of ninety-nine over one hundred, the answer is five feet eleven point six inches. <<WRITE_ANSWER:L' = 5 feet 11.6 inches|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose the rest length of the box is thirty light seconds, and the train T one travels at a speed of zero point eight c. We want to find the time elapsed between the opening of door one and door two in the frame of T one. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Rest length of box = 30 light seconds, train T1 speed = 0.8c. Find the time gap between D1 and D2 opening, in the frame of T1.|id=ex-q-1>> In the frame of T one, the box moves with a speed of zero point eight c, so v over c is zero point eight. That gives us a gamma factor of one divided by the square root of one minus zero point eight squared, which works out to one divided by zero point six. <<WRITE_STEP:v/c = 0.8, so gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - 0.8^2) = 1 / 0.6|id=ex-step-1-1>> In this frame, door two opens after door one. The time elapsed between the openings is given by the formula L times v over c squared, times gamma. <<WRITE_STEP:time gap = L * (v/c^2) * gamma|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we substitute. L is thirty light seconds, which we can write as thirty seconds times c. Then we plug in v as zero point eight c, and gamma as one over zero point six. So we get thirty seconds times c, times zero point eight c, all divided by c squared times zero point six. <<WRITE_STEP:= (30 light seconds * 0.8c) / (c^2 * 0.6) = (30 s)c * 0.8c / (c^2 * 0.6)|id=ex-step-1-3>> The c squared cancels top and bottom, leaving thirty times zero point eight divided by zero point six seconds. And the answer is forty seconds. <<WRITE_ANSWER:time elapsed = 40 seconds|id=ex-ans-1>> And notice, it <<FOCUS:rod-moving+velocity>> only shrinks along the direction it moves. <<FOCUS:rod-rest>> Across its motion, nothing changes. <<WRITE_TEXT:Shrinks only along the motion|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> That sideways agreement is exactly what the relativity principle demands. So both clocks and rods were honest tools, yet motion bends what they read. Moving clocks run slow, moving rods grow short, and the same little factor, square root of one minus v squared over c squared, governs both. We never notice it because v is tiny compared with c. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_4:gamma_runaway>> Push a particle with a steady force forever, and Newton promises it just keeps speeding up, faster and faster, with <<TRACE:newton-line>> no ceiling at all. But nature has <<FOCUS:light-wall>> hung a wall in the sky, the speed of light, and nothing made of matter ever gets through it. <<SECTION:Dynamics at large velocity|id=sec-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> So something in the old rule must bend. The rule we are bending is the one you have trusted for years, force equals mass times acceleration. Here is the honest question. If a constant force never stops pushing, why does the particle refuse to break the light barrier? Where does all that pushing go? <<PAUSE:long>> The secret is momentum. Because the particle starts from rest and the force always points the same way, the motion is along one direction only. segments.narration_chapter: There is a furnace inside the pencil on your desk; if you could unlock the energy hiding in just one gram of it, you could power a small town for days. <<SECTION:Mass is energy|id=sec-1>> The reason is one of the strangest discoveries in all of physics: mass and energy are not two different things, they are two names for exactly the same thing. <<PAUSE:short>> Einstein found that any lump of mass already holds an enormous store of energy, just by existing, and the amount is the mass multiplied by the speed of light squared. <<PAUSE:short>> And here is why the number is so huge: the speed of light is three hundred million meters per second, so squaring it gives a colossal factor, which is why a speck of matter hides a town-sized furnace. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_5:mass_energy_ledger>> Now let me show you where this energy lives, because a particle has <<FOCUS:rest-energy-segment+kinetic-energy-segment>> two kinds of it stacked together. <<WRITE_TEXT:rest energy = m-naught c squared|id=text-rest>> Even a particle sitting perfectly still, doing nothing, owns <<FOCUS:rest-energy-segment>> this left chunk: its rest energy, the mass it has at rest times the speed of light squared. <<UNFOCUS>> A particle at rest still holds energy equal to its rest mass times the speed of light squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:E_0 = m_0 c^2|id=eq-1|boxed>> But watch what happens <<FOCUS:push-arrow>> when I push it; I do work on it, and that work has to go somewhere. <<UNFOCUS>> So here is the puzzle: if I keep pushing a particle to make it faster and faster, the energy I pour in keeps growing without limit, but energy is mass, so what happens to the mass? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The mass actually grows; the faster it moves, the heavier it gets, because the extra energy I gave it shows up as extra mass, which is exactly <<FOCUS:kinetic-energy-segment>> this growing right-hand chunk. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Total energy = rest energy + kinetic energy|id=key-split>> So <<FOCUS:total-energy-bar>> the whole bar is the total energy: the rest energy it always had, plus the kinetic energy of its motion. <<PAUSE:short>> And the beautiful part: when the speed is small compared to light, this extra kinetic chunk shrinks down to exactly the <<FOCUS:kinetic-seg-math>> one-half m v squared you already learned, so relativity contains your old physics inside it. <<UNFOCUS>> The total energy is the rest energy plus, for small speeds, the familiar one-half mass times velocity squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:E = \frac{m_0 c^2}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} = m_0 c^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_0 v^2 + \cdots|id=eq-2|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose a mass of three point six grams, that is three point six times ten to the minus three kilograms, is fully converted into energy. The question asks: how many kilowatt hours of electrical energy will we obtain? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A mass of 3.6 g is fully converted into energy. How many kilowatt hours are obtained?|id=ex-q-1>> Energy and momentum lock together, and for light with no rest mass this leaves energy equal to momentum times the speed of light. <<WRITE_EQUATION:E^2 = m_0^2 c^4 + p^2 c^2|id=eq-3|boxed>> We start from Einstein's relation, <<FOCUS:total-label>> energy equals m times c squared, where c is the speed of light, three times ten to the eighth meters per second. <<WRITE_EQUATION:E = mc^2|id=ex-eq-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now we substitute the numbers. We put in three point six times ten to the minus three kilograms for the mass, and three times ten to the eighth meters per second for c, then square that speed. <<WRITE_STEP:E = (3.6 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{kg})(3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s})^2|id=ex-step-1-1>> Multiplying everything out, the energy comes to thirty-two point four times ten to the thirteenth joules. <<WRITE_STEP:E = 32.4 \times 10^{13}\ \text{J}|id=ex-step-1-2>> To convert to kilowatt hours, recall that one kilowatt hour equals ten to the third joules per second times three thousand six hundred seconds, which is three point six times ten to the sixth joules. So we divide our energy by that. <<WRITE_STEP:1\ \text{kWh} = 10^3\ \text{J/s} \times 3600\ \text{s} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}|id=ex-step-1-3>> Dividing thirty-two point four times ten to the thirteenth joules by three point six times ten to the sixth joules, the answer is nine times ten to the seventh kilowatt hours. <<WRITE_ANSWER:E = 9 \times 10^{7}\ \text{kWh}|id=ex-ans-1>> <<WRITE_TEXT:photon: no rest mass, all energy|id=text-photon>> One last wonder: a particle of light has no rest mass at all, so <<FOCUS:rest-energy-segment>> its left chunk vanishes; it is pure energy and pure momentum, with energy equal to its momentum times the speed of light. <<UNFOCUS>> Remember this: mass and energy are one single thing, and the rule that ties everything together is energy equals m times c squared. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_6:cause_effect_frames>> Picture a frame where a bullet smashes into the bird before the trigger is even pulled, or a dog dies before it is ever born. That is the absurd world we have to rule out. Here is where it comes from. Earlier we kept pushing on a particle, expecting it to go faster and faster forever, but its speed crept toward one wall and never crossed it: the speed of light, c, about three hundred thousand kilometers per second. <<SECTION:The cosmic speed limit|id=sec-1>> <<WRITE_KEY:Nothing exceeds c, about 300000 kilometers per second|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Any speed v of a particle or signal must stay below the speed of light c, which is about three hundred million meters per second. <<WRITE_EQUATION:v < c \approx 3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now you might ask: why should nature care so fiercely about this one number? Why not just let something, anything, go a little bit faster? <<PAUSE:long>> The answer is about cause and effect. Let me set up two observers. <<FOCUS:frame-rest>> Here is me, at rest, with <<FOCUS:frame-rest-space>> space across and <<FOCUS:frame-rest-time>> time going up. And here is a friend <<FOCUS:frame-moving+velocity-arrow>> gliding past to the right at a steady speed v. <<UNFOCUS>> Relativity insists the laws of physics look exactly the same for both of us. Now suppose I fire off a signal that beats light to its target. <<FOCUS:cause-event>> The cause is here, <<FOCUS:effect-event>> the effect is over there, and <<TRACE:faster-than-light-signal>> the line between them is almost flat because the signal is so fast. <<WRITE_TEXT:cause then effect, in my frame|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> In my frame, fine: cause first, then effect. But watch what my moving friend sees, because in relativity <<FOCUS:frame-moving-time+frame-moving>> space and time tilt together when you change frames. <<PAUSE:short>> For a signal faster than light, that tilt is enough to flip the order: my friend sees <<FOCUS:effect-event+cause-event>> the effect happen before the cause. <<UNFOCUS>> The bird is hit before the trigger moves. That is the impossible world. So the speed limit is not a stubborn rule about how engines work. It is nature protecting cause and effect: if effect can never come before its cause in any frame, then c must be <<FOCUS:light-cone-line>> the ultimate speed. <<WRITE_KEY:Limit protects cause before effect|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> And this is bigger than bullets and birds. No particle, no message, no influence of any kind can outrun light, because all of them would break this same chain of cause and effect. <<PAUSE:short>> Now here is a delicious loophole. Physicists asked: what about particles that are born already faster than light and can never slow below it? They called them tachyons. In their hypothetical world effect always precedes cause, and crucially they could never interact with us, so our cause and effect stays safe. Whether tachyons truly exist is still an open question. So remember this: light's speed, about three hundred thousand kilometers per second, is the universe's ultimate speed limit, and nature enforces it not out of stubbornness but to keep every cause safely ahead of its effect. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_7:twin_journey>> Two twins, the same age. One blasts off to a far planet and races back, and when he steps out of the ship he is younger than his brother. Not a trick, not a feeling, genuinely younger. <<SECTION:The set-up|id=sec-1>> <<FOCUS:earth>> Here is Earth, and <<FOCUS:planet>> way over here is a distant planet sitting still, eight light-years away. <<FOCUS:balram-clock>> Balram stays home; <<FOCUS:ram-clock>> Ram takes the trip. Ram <<TRACE:outbound-path>> rides one ship out at eight tenths the speed of light, and at the planet he leaps onto a <<TRACE:return-path>> second ship heading straight back, again at eight tenths the speed of light. <<UNFOCUS>> Now here is the strange thing we learned earlier: when something moves that fast, its clocks run slow. <<FOCUS:ram-clock>> Ram's watch, his heartbeat, even his breathing, all slow down. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The amount a moving clock slows down is captured by one number, called the time-dilation factor, gamma. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> How slow? We package the slowdown into one number called gamma, the time-dilation factor. At eight tenths of light speed it works out to exactly six tenths. Let's count from Balram's chair on Earth. For him, the planet is eight light-years away and Ram crawls there at eight tenths light speed, so <<FOCUS:outbound-path>> the trip out takes ten years. <<PAUSE:long>> <<WRITE_STEP:Earth sees outbound 10 years, return 10 years, total 20 years|id=step-1>> The return is <<FOCUS:return-path>> another ten years. So <<FOCUS:balram-clock>> Balram waits twenty whole years for his brother to come home. <<UNFOCUS>> The time that passes for the travelling twin equals the time on Earth multiplied by the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:t_{\text{Ram}} = t_{\text{Balram}} \times \sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> But Ram's clock ran slow the entire flight. Multiply Balram's twenty years by six tenths, and <<FOCUS:ram-clock>> only twelve years passed for Ram. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Ram ages 12 years, Balram ages 20 years|id=key-1>> So when Ram climbs out, <<FOCUS:ram-clock+balram-clock>> he has aged twelve years while Balram has aged twenty. <<UNFOCUS>> Ram really is eight years younger. <<SECTION:Where is the paradox?|id=sec-2>> Now, you should be itching to object. Motion is relative! From Ram's seat, it is Balram and the whole Earth that flew away and came back. Shouldn't Balram be the younger one? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here is the resolution. Look at the trip: <<FOCUS:turnaround>> only Ram turns around at the planet. <<UNFOCUS>> He jumps ships, he reverses, he switches from one moving frame to another. <<FOCUS:earth>> Balram never does anything but sit still. <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter, the twin paradox worked out with simple numbers.
