lesson_plans.title: The Principle of Relativity

hook.text: You are reading this while hurtling through space at thirty kilometers per second around the Sun. So why can you pour a glass of water without spilling a single drop?

crucial_facts: No experiment done inside a smoothly moving system can tell you whether you are moving or standing still.
There is no preferred frame of reference; all motion at constant velocity is purely relative.

diagrams.purpose: Show a platform observer at rest and a train observer gliding by at constant velocity, with the same dropped-stone event marked in both, so the student sees the two equivalent points of view.

required_elements.description: The platform frame at rest: a horizontal ground line with a standing person on the left and labelled axes x and y.
The train frame, a railway car drawn to the right of the platform person, with its own person inside and primed axes x-prime and y-prime.
A horizontal arrow on the train pointing right, labelled v, showing the train's constant velocity relative to the platform.
A short straight vertical dashed path from the platform person's hand down to their left foot.
A short straight vertical dashed path from the train person's hand down to their left foot, identical in shape to the platform one.

choreography.narration: You are reading this while hurtling through space at thirty kilometers per second around the Sun. So why can you pour a glass of water without spilling a single drop?

<<SECTION:The Principle of Relativity|id=sec-1>>Here is the answer, and it is one of the deepest ideas in all of physics. Steady motion, motion with no jerks and no turning, simply cannot be felt from the inside.
Picture yourself standing on a railway platform. You drop a stone, and it lands neatly on your left foot.
Now climb aboard a train that is gliding past at a steady one hundred twenty kilometers per hour, and let it slide along to the right.
Drop the very same stone inside that moving train. Where does it land? Right on your left foot, exactly as before. Nothing is different.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Inertial frame = steady velocity, no jerks|id=text-1>>A point of view from which you measure motion is called a frame of reference, and one moving at a steady velocity, with no acceleration, is called an inertial frame.
Now, here is the interesting thing. Could any experiment whatsoever, done sealed inside that train, reveal that you are moving?

<<WRITE_KEY:No experiment inside tells you if you are moving|id=key-1>>The answer is no. Not the stone, not a swinging pendulum, not a thrown ball. No experiment inside can ever tell you whether the train is parked at the platform or racing across the country.
The reason is that Newton's law keeps exactly the same form in every inertial frame: force always equals mass times acceleration, on the platform and on the train alike.
Since identical experiments are governed by identical laws, they must give identical results, no matter which frame you are sitting in.
<<WRITE_KEY:No preferred frame: all motion is relative|id=key-2>>So there is no special, preferred frame that nature calls truly at rest. Every smoothly moving frame is just as good as any other.
You may call the platform at rest and the train moving, or the train at rest and the platform moving. Both stories are equally true, because all motion at constant velocity is purely relative.

lesson_plans.title: Are Maxwell's Laws the Same for Everyone?

hook.text: Two friends start at the very same spot. One stays put, the other races off to the right at half the speed of light. They both watch the same flash of light fly away — and they both measure it pulling away from them at exactly the same speed. How can that possibly be true?

crucial_facts: Maxwell's laws look the same in every frame moving at constant speed, which forces light to travel at the same speed c for every observer, no matter how fast they themselves are moving.
If everyone measures the same speed for light, then their clocks cannot agree — what is one moment in time for one observer is not the same moment for another.

diagrams.purpose: Show observer A at rest, observer B moving right at half c, and the light pulse W, so the student can see why A measures the same speed for the light that B does — the heart of the paradox.

required_elements.description: Observer A, standing still at the origin on the left.
Observer B, who starts at the origin with A and slides to the right.
An arrow on B pointing right, labelled one half c, showing B's motion.
The light flash W, drawn as a bright dot racing to the right ahead of both observers.
A label showing the light pulling away from A at speed c.
A label showing the light ALSO pulling away from B at speed c.

choreography.narration: Two friends start at the very same spot. One stays put, the other races off to the right at half the speed of light. They both watch the same flash of light fly away — and they both measure it pulling away at exactly the same speed. How can that possibly be true?

<<SECTION:Maxwell and the speed of light|id=sec-1>>To see where this puzzle comes from, we need Maxwell's laws — the rules of electricity and magnetism. Buried inside them is a number: the speed of light through empty space, about three hundred million meters per second, which we call c.

Now here is the big question. We already believe the laws of physics look the same to anyone moving at a steady speed — inside a smoothly gliding ship you cannot tell you are moving at all. So do Maxwell's laws look the same to everyone too?

<<WRITE_KEY:Maxwell's laws look the same in every steady-moving frame, so light travels at speed c for everyone|id=key-1>>And the answer, confirmed by experiment, is yes. The very same Maxwell's laws hold for every observer moving at a constant speed. But that has a startling price: the speed of light, c, must come out the same for all of them.
Let me show you why that feels impossible. Here is observer A, standing still. At the very first instant, A, observer B, and a flash of light W are all together at one spot.
Now let B slide off to the right at half the speed of light, while the flash races to the right at the full speed of light, leaving everyone behind.

Here is the everyday answer you would expect. Since B is chasing after the light, surely the light should pull away from B more slowly than it pulls away from the stationary A. That is just common sense, like a fast car gaining on a slow one.

<<WRITE_TEXT:A measures c. B also measures c.|id=text-1>>But nature refuses. A measures the light leaving at speed c — and B, even while chasing it at half c, also measures it leaving at the full speed c. The same flash, the same speed, for both of them.

<<WRITE_KEY:Same speed for everyone means their clocks cannot agree|id=key-2>>Sit with how strange that is. If A and B both started together, and both see the light always exactly the same distance ahead at every tick, then the simple idea that distances just add up must break.
So which piece of common sense has to give way? Something we never doubted must be quietly wrong.

Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose B moves away from A at speed u equals c over two, toward the right. A light pulse, call it W, moves at speed c toward the right relative to both A and B. And at time zero, A, B, and W are all at the same place. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: B moves right at u = c/2; pulse W moves right at c relative to both A and B; at t=0 all at same place. Does AW = AB + BW?|id=ex-q-1>>

Each observer keeps a diary of distances over time. In A's diary: at one second AB is one point five times ten to the eighth meters and AW is three times ten to the eighth meters; at two seconds AB is three times ten to the eighth meters and AW is six times ten to the eighth meters; at three seconds AB is four point five times ten to the eighth meters and AW is nine times ten to the eighth meters. <<WRITE_STEP:A's diary: t=1s -> AB=1.5e8 m, AW=3e8 m; t=2s -> AB=3e8 m, AW=6e8 m; t=3s -> AB=4.5e8 m, AW=9e8 m|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Now B's diary shows the same numbers: BA equals AB and BW equals AW at each time. So at every instant we find AW equals BW even though AB is not zero. <<WRITE_STEP:B's diary: BA = AB and BW = AW at each t, so AW = BW while AB != 0|id=ex-step-1-2>>

But ordinary thinking says AW should equal AB plus BW. Here that relation simply does not hold, because both observers measure the pulse moving away at the same speed c. The two diaries suggest something is wrong with our everyday rule of adding distances. <<WRITE_ANSWER:The expected relation AW = AB + BW fails; both A and B see W move at speed c, so simple distance addition breaks down.|id=ex-ans-1>>

It is time itself. The only way everyone can agree on the speed of light is if they disagree on time — one second for A is simply not the same second for B. What feels like a single moment for one observer is not one moment for the other.

And that is the doorway into relativity. We held onto Maxwell's laws and the speed of light for every observer — and in return we had to give up the idea that time ticks the same for everyone. Next, we will see exactly how clocks and rulers must change to keep this promise.

equations.explanation_in_words: Maxwell's laws hide a fixed number for the speed of light: it depends only on two constants of empty space, and it comes out to about three hundred million meters per second.

lesson_plans.title: Kinematical Consequences: Why Moving Clocks Run Slow and Moving Rods Get Shorter

hook.text: Build a clock out of nothing but a flash of light bouncing between two mirrors. Now run past it, and watch something impossible happen: that clock starts ticking slower than yours, even though it is identical.

crucial_facts: A moving clock runs slow by the factor square root of one minus v squared over c squared, because the light pulse inside it must travel a longer diagonal path.
To keep the speed of light the same for everyone, a moving rod shrinks along its direction of motion by that same factor, square root of one minus v squared over c squared.

diagrams.purpose: Show the same light clock at rest (pulse goes straight up) and moving (pulse traces a diagonal), so the right triangle itself derives the time-dilation factor.

required_elements.description: Bottom mirror of the light clock.
Top mirror of the light clock, a fixed distance above the bottom.
The light pulse path straight up and down when the clock is at rest.
The diagonal tent-shaped path of the light pulse when the clock moves to the right.
Horizontal base of the triangle, length v times t, the distance the clock moves.
Hypotenuse of the triangle, length c times t, the diagonal light path.
Vertical leg of the triangle, length c times t-nought, the height between mirrors.

diagrams.purpose: Show a measuring rod at full length in its rest frame and shortened in the moving frame, along the direction of motion only.

required_elements.description: The measuring rod at full length L-nought in its own rest frame.
The same rod seen moving, shortened along its direction of motion.
Label showing the contracted length equals L-nought times the relativity factor.

choreography.narration: Build a clock out of nothing but a flash of light bouncing between two mirrors, one on the bottom and one on top. Every round trip is one tick.
<<SECTION:The light clock|id=sec-1>>Sitting still, the pulse just goes straight up to the top mirror and straight back down. Simple, honest, and the time for one tick we will call t-nought.
Now here is the interesting thing. Suppose I run past this clock, or what is the same, the clock glides past me to the right at speed v.
While the light travels from the bottom mirror up to the top, the whole clock has moved sideways. So from where I stand, the pulse does not go straight up. It goes along a slanted, diagonal path.

Look closely and you will see a right triangle hiding here. The bottom side is how far the clock moved, v times t. The slanted side is the path the light took, and the upright side is the same mirror gap as before.
Now the crucial fact that nature forces on us: the speed of light is the same for everyone. So that long diagonal path was also covered at speed c, which means the slanted side has length c times t.
Here is the puzzle. The light in the moving clock had a longer road to travel, but it is forbidden from going any faster. So what has to give?

<<WRITE_KEY:Moving clock runs slow by the factor root of one minus v squared over c squared|id=key-1>>Time itself must stretch. Pythagoras on this triangle gives c times t for the slanted side, squared, equals v times t squared plus c times t-nought squared, and out pops the factor square root of one minus v squared over c squared. The moving clock ticks slower.

Say it plainly, because it is strange: a moving clock runs slow, by exactly that square root of one minus v squared over c squared. And it is not a trick of this clock. Every clock, even your heartbeat, must agree.
<<SECTION:Length contraction|id=sec-2>>Now if time gets squeezed, something else must give too. Picture a measuring rod lying still in its own frame, at its full, honest length L-nought.
When that same rod flies past you along its own length, to keep the speed of light coming out the same for everyone, the rod must appear shorter, shrunk by that very same factor.

Here's an example from the chapter. A person on a train moving at three times ten to the seventh meters per second goes to sleep at ten p.m. by his watch and gets up at four a.m. That's six hours of sleep on his watch. The question is: how long did he sleep according to the clocks at the stations? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Train at 3e7 m/s; sleeps 10 p.m. to 4 a.m. on his watch. How long per station clocks?|id=ex-q-1>>

First, let's identify which time is which. Both events, falling asleep and waking up, are recorded by the single watch he carries, so the watch reading is the proper time interval. That proper time is six hours. <<WRITE_STEP:Watch reading = proper time, delta t = 6 hours|id=ex-step-1-1>>

The station clocks belong to the ground frame, and in that frame he falls asleep at one place and wakes up at another. So the station clocks give the improper time interval, which is longer. We get it by multiplying by the gamma factor: delta t prime equals gamma times delta t, which is delta t over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Station clocks = improper time, delta t' = delta t / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Now we put in the numbers. The speed v is three times ten to the seventh meters per second, and the speed of light c is three times ten to the eighth meters per second. So v over c is one tenth. Squaring that gives one hundredth, and one minus one hundredth leaves ninety-nine hundredths under the root. <<WRITE_STEP:v/c = 1/10, so delta t' = 6 h / sqrt(1 - 1/100) = 6 h * sqrt(100/99)|id=ex-step-1-3>>

The gamma factor is therefore the square root of one hundred over ninety-nine. Multiplying six hours by that factor, the sleep duration in the ground frame comes out to six hours and one point eight minutes. <<WRITE_ANSWER:delta t' = 6 hours 1.8 minutes|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. A passenger lies in a train with his head toward the engine and feet toward the guard's coach, so his body is measured parallel to the direction of motion. In the train frame he measures six feet tall, and the train moves past the ground at a speed of c divided by ten. The question is: how tall does he appear in the ground frame? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Passenger is 6 ft in train frame, train moves at c/10. Height in ground frame?|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by noting that the six feet is the rest length, since the passenger is at rest in the train. In the ground frame he is moving, so his length parallel to the motion is contracted. Here v over c is one tenth, so the contraction factor is the square root of one minus one tenth squared, which is the square root of ninety-nine over one hundred. <<WRITE_STEP:L' = 6 ft × \u221a(1 - (1/10)\u00b2) = 6 ft × \u221a(99/100)|id=ex-step-1-1>>
Multiplying six feet by the square root of ninety-nine over one hundred, the answer is five feet eleven point six inches. <<WRITE_ANSWER:L' = 5 feet 11.6 inches|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose the rest length of the box is thirty light seconds, and the train T one travels at a speed of zero point eight c. We want to find the time elapsed between the opening of door one and door two in the frame of T one. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Rest length of box = 30 light seconds, train T1 speed = 0.8c. Find the time gap between D1 and D2 opening, in the frame of T1.|id=ex-q-1>>

In the frame of T one, the box moves with a speed of zero point eight c, so v over c is zero point eight. That gives us a gamma factor of one divided by the square root of one minus zero point eight squared, which works out to one divided by zero point six. <<WRITE_STEP:v/c = 0.8, so gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - 0.8^2) = 1 / 0.6|id=ex-step-1-1>>

In this frame, door two opens after door one. The time elapsed between the openings is given by the formula L times v over c squared, times gamma. <<WRITE_STEP:time gap = L * (v/c^2) * gamma|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Now we substitute. L is thirty light seconds, which we can write as thirty seconds times c. Then we plug in v as zero point eight c, and gamma as one over zero point six. So we get thirty seconds times c, times zero point eight c, all divided by c squared times zero point six. <<WRITE_STEP:= (30 light seconds * 0.8c) / (c^2 * 0.6) = (30 s)c * 0.8c / (c^2 * 0.6)|id=ex-step-1-3>>
The c squared cancels top and bottom, leaving thirty times zero point eight divided by zero point six seconds. And the answer is forty seconds. <<WRITE_ANSWER:time elapsed = 40 seconds|id=ex-ans-1>>

And notice, it only shrinks along the direction it moves. Across its motion, nothing changes. <<WRITE_TEXT:Shrinks only along the motion|id=text-1>>That sideways agreement is exactly what the relativity principle demands.

So both clocks and rods were honest tools, yet motion bends what they read. Moving clocks run slow, moving rods grow short, and the same little factor, square root of one minus v squared over c squared, governs both. We never notice it because v is tiny compared with c.

equations.explanation_in_words: The slanted light path squared equals the sideways distance squared plus the mirror gap squared, just Pythagoras on the triangle we drew.
Solving that triangle for the time tells us the moving clock's tick is the resting tick divided by the square root of one minus v squared over c squared.
The moving rod's length is its rest length multiplied by that same square root of one minus v squared over c squared.

lesson_plans.title: Dynamics at Large Velocity: Why You Can't Reach the Speed of Light

hook.text: Push a particle with a steady force, forever, and Newton swears it should speed up without limit. Yet nature draws a wall it can never cross: the speed of light. So what gives way?

crucial_facts: A moving particle's momentum is its rest mass times gamma times its velocity, so as it nears the speed of light its inertia blows up and no force can push it past c.

The gamma factor, one over the square root of one minus v-squared over c-squared, is tiny-close to one at everyday speeds, which is why Newton's law works perfectly until you approach the speed of light.

diagrams.purpose: Show momentum climbing toward infinity as speed approaches c, even though velocity is capped — the visual reason the speed of light is a wall.

required_elements.description: Horizontal axis labelled speed, running from zero up to c marked at the right edge with a vertical dashed wall.
Vertical axis labelled momentum, running upward.
A straight line through the origin showing Newton's prediction, momentum proportional to speed, climbing steadily.
The relativistic curve that hugs the Newton line at low speed then bends sharply upward, shooting toward infinity as speed approaches c.
A vertical dashed line at speed equals c, the wall the curve never crosses.
A shaded patch near the origin where the two curves overlap, the everyday regime where Newton is right.

choreography.narration: Push a particle with a steady force forever, and Newton promises it just keeps speeding up, faster and faster, with no ceiling at all. But nature has hung a wall in the sky, the speed of light, and nothing made of matter ever gets through it.
<<SECTION:Dynamics at large velocity|id=sec-1>>So something in the old rule must bend. The rule we are bending is the one you have trusted for years, force equals mass times acceleration.
Here is the honest question. If a constant force never stops pushing, why does the particle refuse to break the light barrier? Where does all that pushing go?
The secret is momentum. In Newton's world momentum is simply mass times velocity, so push harder and it grows without limit, a perfectly straight line climbing forever.

<<WRITE_TEXT:gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)|id=text-gamma>>But relativity inserts a new character into the formula, a number we call gamma, equal to one over the square root of one minus the velocity squared over the speed of light squared.

Now here is the lovely part. At everyday speeds, walking, driving, even rocketing into orbit, v over c is so tiny that gamma is almost exactly one, so the relativistic curve lies right on top of Newton's line.
That overlap is why Newton's law has worked flawlessly for three centuries. In this whole shaded region the two pictures simply agree.
So the real momentum of a particle is its rest mass times gamma times its velocity. The rest mass is just the ordinary mass you would measure standing still beside it.

And watch what gamma does as the speed creeps toward the speed of light. The bottom of that fraction, the square root, shrinks toward zero, so gamma swells toward infinity, and the momentum shoots straight up.

So now we can answer where the pushing goes. The force keeps adding momentum, but because gamma is exploding, almost all of that momentum goes into making the particle harder to accelerate, not faster.

Here's an example from the chapter. A particle starts at rest at the origin, and a constant force F begins acting on it at time t equals zero. Because the particle starts from rest and the force always points the same way, the motion is along one direction only. We want the speed of the particle at time t. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Particle at rest at origin, constant force F from t=0. Find speed v at time t.|id=ex-q-1>>
We start from the equation of motion, which says the rate of change of momentum equals F. That is, d p by d t equals F. <<WRITE_STEP:dp/dt = F|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Now we integrate both sides. The integral of d p from zero to p equals the integral of F d t from zero to t. Since F is constant, this gives p equals F times t. <<WRITE_STEP:∫₀ᵖ dp = ∫₀ᵗ F dt  →  p = Ft|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Now we put in the relativistic momentum: p equals m naught times v divided by the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. Setting that equal to F times t gives m naught v over square root of one minus v squared over c squared equals F times t. <<WRITE_STEP:m₀v / √(1 − v²/c²) = Ft|id=ex-step-1-3>>

Solving this for v, we find v equals F times t times c divided by the square root of m naught squared c squared plus F squared t squared. Notice that however large t may be, v can never exceed c. No matter how long you apply the force, the speed stays less than the speed of light. <<WRITE_ANSWER:v = Ftc / √(m₀²c² + F²t²),  v < c always|id=ex-ans-1>>

<<WRITE_KEY:p = m0 * gamma * v -> infinite inertia as v -> c|id=key-momentum>>That growing gamma acts like a growing inertia. Near the speed of light the particle behaves as if its mass is enormous, so no finite force can ever shove it across the wall.

And the law of motion itself is gentler than you might fear. We simply say force equals the rate of change of this relativistic momentum, and if no force acts, that momentum stays perfectly constant, just like before.

equations.explanation_in_words: Relativity inserts a number gamma equal to one over the square root of one minus the velocity squared over the speed of light squared.
The real momentum of a particle is its rest mass times gamma times its velocity.
The law of motion says force equals the rate of change of this relativistic momentum.

lesson_plans.title: Energy and Momentum: Mass Is Bottled-Up Energy

hook.text: There is a furnace inside the pencil on your desk. If you could unlock the energy hiding in just one gram of it, you could power a small town for days.

crucial_facts: Mass and energy are two names for the same thing; the energy locked in a mass is that mass times the speed of light squared.
Pushing a particle gives it energy, and because energy IS mass, the particle actually gets heavier as it speeds up.

diagrams.purpose: Show total energy splitting into rest energy plus kinetic energy, so E equals m c squared is seen as rest energy plus the everyday one-half m v squared.

required_elements.description: A tall horizontal bar labelled E, the total energy of a moving particle.
The left portion of the total bar, labelled rest energy, representing m-naught c squared.
The right portion of the total bar, labelled kinetic energy, representing the extra energy gained by motion.
A small stationary particle drawn at left with a tiny mass label m-naught, sitting beside the rest-energy segment.
The same particle drawn moving fast to the right with a velocity arrow and a larger mass label m, sitting above the full bar.
An arrow pushing the moving particle, indicating work being done that adds to the kinetic-energy segment.

choreography.narration: There is a furnace inside the pencil on your desk; if you could unlock the energy hiding in just one gram of it, you could power a small town for days.
<<SECTION:Mass is energy|id=sec-1>>The reason is one of the strangest discoveries in all of physics: mass and energy are not two different things, they are two names for exactly the same thing.
Einstein found that any lump of mass already holds an enormous store of energy, just by existing, and the amount is the mass multiplied by the speed of light squared.

And here is why the number is so huge: the speed of light is three hundred million meters per second, so squaring it gives a colossal factor, which is why a speck of matter hides a town-sized furnace.
Now let me show you where this energy lives, because a particle has two kinds of it stacked together.

<<WRITE_TEXT:rest energy = m-naught c squared|id=text-rest>>Even a particle sitting perfectly still, doing nothing, owns this left chunk: its rest energy, the mass it has at rest times the speed of light squared.
But watch what happens when I push it; I do work on it, and that work has to go somewhere.
So here is the puzzle: if I keep pushing a particle to make it faster and faster, the energy I pour in keeps growing without limit, but energy is mass, so what happens to the mass?
The mass actually grows; the faster it moves, the heavier it gets, because the extra energy I gave it shows up as extra mass, which is exactly this growing right-hand chunk.
<<WRITE_KEY:Total energy = rest energy + kinetic energy|id=key-split>>So the whole bar is the total energy: the rest energy it always had, plus the kinetic energy of its motion.

And the beautiful part: when the speed is small compared to light, this extra kinetic chunk shrinks down to exactly the one-half m v squared you already learned, so relativity contains your old physics inside it.

Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose a mass of three point six grams, that is three point six times ten to the minus three kilograms, is fully converted into energy. The question asks: how many kilowatt hours of electrical energy will we obtain? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A mass of 3.6 g is fully converted into energy. How many kilowatt hours are obtained?|id=ex-q-1>>
We start from Einstein's relation, energy equals m times c squared, where c is the speed of light, three times ten to the eighth meters per second. <<WRITE_EQUATION:E = mc^2|id=ex-eq-1>>

Now we substitute the numbers. We put in three point six times ten to the minus three kilograms for the mass, and three times ten to the eighth meters per second for c, then square that speed. <<WRITE_STEP:E = (3.6 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{kg})(3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s})^2|id=ex-step-1-1>>
Multiplying everything out, the energy comes to thirty-two point four times ten to the thirteenth joules. <<WRITE_STEP:E = 32.4 \times 10^{13}\ \text{J}|id=ex-step-1-2>>

To convert to kilowatt hours, recall that one kilowatt hour equals ten to the third joules per second times three thousand six hundred seconds, which is three point six times ten to the sixth joules. So we divide our energy by that. <<WRITE_STEP:1\ \text{kWh} = 10^3\ \text{J/s} \times 3600\ \text{s} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}|id=ex-step-1-3>>

Dividing thirty-two point four times ten to the thirteenth joules by three point six times ten to the sixth joules, the answer is nine times ten to the seventh kilowatt hours. <<WRITE_ANSWER:E = 9 \times 10^{7}\ \text{kWh}|id=ex-ans-1>>

<<WRITE_TEXT:photon: no rest mass, all energy|id=text-photon>>One last wonder: a particle of light has no rest mass at all, so its left chunk vanishes; it is pure energy and pure momentum, with energy equal to its momentum times the speed of light.
Remember this: mass and energy are one single thing, and the rule that ties everything together is energy equals m times c squared.

equations.explanation_in_words: A particle at rest still holds energy equal to its rest mass times the speed of light squared.

equations.latex: E = \frac{m_0 c^2}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} = m_0 c^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_0 v^2 + \cdots
equations.explanation_in_words: The total energy is the rest energy plus, for small speeds, the familiar one-half mass times velocity squared.
Energy and momentum lock together, and for light with no rest mass this leaves energy equal to momentum times the speed of light.

lesson_plans.title: The Ultimate Speed

hook.text: Imagine a frame where a bullet hits the bird before the trigger is ever pulled, or a dog dies before it is born. That nonsense is exactly what nature forbids, and forbidding it is what sets the cosmic speed limit.

crucial_facts: Nothing — no particle and no information — can travel faster than light, about three hundred thousand kilometers per second.
The speed limit exists to protect cause and effect: an effect must never come before its cause in any frame.

diagrams.purpose: Show how a faster-than-light signal lets a different observer see the effect arrive before its cause, breaking causality.

required_elements.description: A rest frame with horizontal space axis and vertical time axis, an observer standing at the origin.
A second frame sliding to the right at velocity v, its tilted axes overlaid on the rest frame.
An arrow labelled v showing the moving frame's velocity to the right.
A marked point labelled 'cause' — for example, a trigger being pulled.
A marked point labelled 'effect' — for example, the bird being hit — placed to the right of the cause.
A nearly-horizontal line connecting cause-event to effect-event, representing a signal travelling faster than light.
A diagonal line at forty-five degrees through the cause event marking the speed-of-light limit.

choreography.narration: Picture a frame where a bullet smashes into the bird before the trigger is even pulled, or a dog dies before it is ever born. That is the absurd world we have to rule out.

Here is where it comes from. Earlier we kept pushing on a particle, expecting it to go faster and faster forever, but its speed crept toward one wall and never crossed it: the speed of light, c, about three hundred thousand kilometers per second. <<SECTION:The cosmic speed limit|id=sec-1>><<WRITE_KEY:Nothing exceeds c, about 300000 kilometers per second|id=key-1>>
Now you might ask: why should nature care so fiercely about this one number? Why not just let something, anything, go a little bit faster?
The answer is about cause and effect. Let me set up two observers. Here is me, at rest, with space across and time going up.
And here is a friend gliding past to the right at a steady speed v. Relativity insists the laws of physics look exactly the same for both of us.

Now suppose I fire off a signal that beats light to its target. The cause is here, the effect is over there, and the line between them is almost flat because the signal is so fast. <<WRITE_TEXT:cause then effect, in my frame|id=text-1>>
In my frame, fine: cause first, then effect. But watch what my moving friend sees, because in relativity space and time tilt together when you change frames.
For a signal faster than light, that tilt is enough to flip the order: my friend sees the effect happen before the cause. The bird is hit before the trigger moves. That is the impossible world.

So the speed limit is not a stubborn rule about how engines work. It is nature protecting cause and effect: if effect can never come before its cause in any frame, then c must be the ultimate speed. <<WRITE_KEY:Limit protects cause before effect|id=key-2>>
And this is bigger than bullets and birds. No particle, no message, no influence of any kind can outrun light, because all of them would break this same chain of cause and effect.
Now here is a delicious loophole. Physicists asked: what about particles that are born already faster than light and can never slow below it? They called them tachyons.
In their hypothetical world effect always precedes cause, and crucially they could never interact with us, so our cause and effect stays safe. Whether tachyons truly exist is still an open question.

So remember this: light's speed, about three hundred thousand kilometers per second, is the universe's ultimate speed limit, and nature enforces it not out of stubbornness but to keep every cause safely ahead of its effect.

equations.explanation_in_words: Any speed v of a particle or signal must stay below the speed of light c, which is about three hundred million meters per second.

lesson_plans.title: The Twin Paradox: Why One Twin Comes Home Younger

hook.text: Two twins, the same age. One blasts off to a far planet and races back. He steps out of the ship... and he's younger than his brother. Not a trick. Not a feeling. Genuinely, measurably younger.

crucial_facts: A moving clock runs slow, so the travelling twin ages less than the twin who stays home.
The paradox is broken because only the travelling twin turns around and switches frames, so the two are not interchangeable.

diagrams.purpose: Show the travelling twin's round trip — out to the planet and back — so the asymmetry (the turnaround) is visible and the time-dilation factor can be attached to each leg.

required_elements.description: Earth on the left, where Balram stays the whole time.
A distant planet on the right, at rest relative to Earth, the turnaround point.
Arrow from Earth to the planet representing the outbound spaceship leg at high speed.
Arrow from the planet back to Earth representing the return spaceship leg at high speed.
A marker at the planet highlighting where Ram jumps to the other ship and reverses direction.
A clock label tracking the travelling twin Ram's elapsed time.
A clock label at Earth tracking the stay-home twin Balram's elapsed time.

choreography.narration: Two twins, the same age. One blasts off to a far planet and races back, and when he steps out of the ship he is younger than his brother. Not a trick, not a feeling, genuinely younger.
<<SECTION:The set-up|id=sec-1>>Here is Earth, and way over here is a distant planet sitting still, eight light-years away. Balram stays home; Ram takes the trip.
Ram rides one ship out at eight tenths the speed of light, and at the planet he leaps onto a second ship heading straight back, again at eight tenths the speed of light.
Now here is the strange thing we learned earlier: when something moves that fast, its clocks run slow. Ram's watch, his heartbeat, even his breathing, all slow down.
How slow? We package the slowdown into one number called gamma, the time-dilation factor. At eight tenths of light speed it works out to exactly six tenths.
Let's count from Balram's chair on Earth. For him, the planet is eight light-years away and Ram crawls there at eight tenths light speed, so the trip out takes ten years.
<<WRITE_STEP:Earth sees outbound 10 years, return 10 years, total 20 years|id=step-1>>The return is another ten years. So Balram waits twenty whole years for his brother to come home.
But Ram's clock ran slow the entire flight. Multiply Balram's twenty years by six tenths, and only twelve years passed for Ram.
<<WRITE_KEY:Ram ages 12 years, Balram ages 20 years|id=key-1>>So when Ram climbs out, he has aged twelve years while Balram has aged twenty. Ram really is eight years younger.

<<SECTION:Where is the paradox?|id=sec-2>>Now, you should be itching to object. Motion is relative! From Ram's seat, it is Balram and the whole Earth that flew away and came back. Shouldn't Balram be the younger one?
Here is the resolution. Look at the trip: only Ram turns around at the planet. He jumps ships, he reverses, he switches from one moving frame to another. Balram never does anything but sit still.

Here's an example from the chapter, the twin paradox worked out with simple numbers. The distance between the earth and the planet is eight light-years, measured in the earth frame. Ram's outgoing spaceship S one moves at zero point eight c, and his return spaceship S two also moves at zero point eight c. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Earth-planet distance = 8 light-years; speed of S1 = 0.8c, speed of S2 = 0.8c. Ram travels out and back. How much do Ram and Balram each age?|id=ex-q-1>>

Let's analyse everything from the point of view of Balram, who stays on the earth. For him both spaceships move at zero point eight c, so the time-dilation factor gamma is one over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared, which works out to one over zero point six. <<WRITE_STEP:gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = 1 / 0.6|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Balram first calculates how long the outward trip takes in his own earth frame. That's the distance, eight light-years, divided by the speed, zero point eight c, which gives ten years. <<WRITE_STEP:Earth-frame time one way = 8 light-years / 0.8c = 10 years|id=ex-step-1-2>>

But during all those ten years, time runs slowly on the moving spaceship S one. The ship's clocks read only ten years times zero point six, which is six years for the outbound leg. <<WRITE_STEP:Ship time one way = 10 years x 0.6 = 6 years|id=ex-step-1-3>>

Then Ram jumps into S two for the return journey. Again ten years pass on the earth, but on the spaceship that leg is clocked at only six years. So Ram's total is six plus six, twelve years, while Balram lives through ten plus ten, twenty years. <<WRITE_STEP:Ram total = 6 + 6 = 12 years; Balram total = 10 + 10 = 20 years|id=ex-step-1-4>>

And so the answer is that Ram has aged only twelve years while Balram has aged twenty years, making Ram younger than Balram by eight years. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Ram ages 12 years, Balram ages 20 years - Ram is younger by 8 years|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter on the twin paradox. Let's analyze the journey from the traveling twin Ram's point of view. From Ram's frame, the distance between earth and the planet is not the full eight light-years that Balram measures. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: From Ram's frame, how much younger does he conclude Balram is?|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by contracting the distance. To Ram, the separation shrinks by a factor of zero point six, so the contracted distance is eight light-years times zero point six, which equals four point eight light-years. <<WRITE_STEP:Contracted distance = 8 light-years × 0.6 = 4.8 light-years|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Now, the planet is approaching Ram at zero point eight c. So the time taken for the planet to reach him is four point eight light-years divided by zero point eight c, which gives six years for that leg. <<WRITE_STEP:Time per leg = 4.8 light-years ÷ 0.8c = 6 years|id=ex-step-1-2>>

On the return leg, the earth is again four point eight light-years away approaching at zero point eight c, taking another six years. So according to Ram's clock, his total trip was twelve years. <<WRITE_STEP:Total trip on Ram's clock = 6 + 6 = 12 years|id=ex-step-1-3>>

Here's where the paradox bites. As twelve years pass on Ram's clock, he calculates that Balram's clock advanced only twelve years times zero point six, which is seven point two years. <<WRITE_STEP:Balram's clock = 12 years × 0.6 = 7.2 years|id=ex-step-1-4>>

So from Ram's analysis, Balram should be twelve minus seven point two, which is four point eight years younger than him. Each twin thinks the other is younger, and that is the paradox. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Ram concludes Balram is 12 − 7.2 = 4.8 years younger|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter that resolves the twin paradox. The captain tells Ram: planet P is four point eight light-years away, contracted in our frame, and it's coming towards us at zero point eight c, so it will take six years on his clock for the planet to reach us. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Contracted distance 4.8 light-years, planet approaches at 0.8c, reaching Ram in 6 years. Resolve the twin paradox.|id=ex-q-1>>

Ram works out the first piece. The clocks on the earth and on the planet will advance by six years times zero point six, which is three point six years, by the time the planet reaches us. <<WRITE_STEP:Earth & planet clocks advance = 6 years × 0.6 = 3.6 years|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Now the captain explains the synchronization. In Ram's frame S one, the planet's clock is at the rear end, so it's running six point four years ahead of the earth's clock. When the earth's clock read zero, the planet's clock already read six point four years. <<WRITE_STEP:In S1: planet clock leads by 6.4 years (planet at rear)|id=ex-step-1-2>>

As the planet reaches us, both clocks advance by those three point six years. So when you jump out of frame S one, the earth's clock reads three point six years, but the planet's clock reads ten years. <<WRITE_STEP:Leaving S1: earth clock = 3.6 years, planet clock = 6.4 + 3.6 = 10 years|id=ex-step-1-3>>

Now you board frame S two, and the commander explains the flip. In this frame it is the earth's clock that leads by six point four years. The planet's clock reads ten years, so the earth's clock must read sixteen point four years. <<WRITE_STEP:Entering S2: earth clock leads by 6.4 years → earth reads 10 + 6.4 = 16.4 years|id=ex-step-1-4>>

During the six years you spend on S two heading back, the earth's clock advances another three point six years, reaching twenty years. The traveler aged less, and the paradox is resolved. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Earth clock = 16.4 + 3.6 = 20 years — paradox resolved.|id=ex-ans-1>>
<<WRITE_TEXT:only the traveller switches frames|id=text-1>>That turnaround makes the twins genuinely different. They are not interchangeable, so there is no contradiction, only an honest answer.
So the rule stands: the moving clock runs slow, and because only Ram did the travelling and the turning, Ram is the one who comes home young.

equations.explanation_in_words: The amount a moving clock slows down is captured by one number, called the time-dilation factor, gamma.
The time that passes for the travelling twin equals the time on Earth multiplied by the square root of one minus v squared over c squared.

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Inertial frame = steady velocity, no jerks|id=text-1>>A point of view from which you measure motion is called a frame of reference, and one moving at a steady velocity, with no acceleration, is called an inertial frame.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Maxwell and the speed of light|id=sec-1>>To see where this puzzle comes from, we need Maxwell's laws — the rules of electricity and magnetism. segments.raw_narration: It is time itself. The only way everyone can agree on the speed of light is if they disagree on time — one second for A is simply not the same second for B. What feels like a single moment for one observer is not one moment for the other.

segments.raw_narration: Build a clock out of nothing but a flash of light bouncing between two mirrors, one on the bottom and one on top. Every round trip is one tick.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:The light clock|id=sec-1>>Sitting still, the pulse just goes straight up to the top mirror and straight back down. Simple, honest, and the time for one tick we will call t-nought.

segments.raw_narration: Now here is the interesting thing. Suppose I run past this clock, or what is the same, the clock glides past me to the right at speed v.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:base-vt>> Now here is the interesting thing. Suppose I run past this clock, or what is the same, the clock glides past me to the right at speed v. <<POINT:base-vt>>

segments.raw_narration: While the light travels from the bottom mirror up to the top, the whole clock has moved sideways. So from where I stand, the pulse does not go straight up. It goes along a slanted, diagonal path.

segments.raw_narration: Look closely and you will see a right triangle hiding here. The bottom side is how far the clock moved, v times t. The slanted side is the path the light took, and the upright side is the same mirror gap as before.

segments.raw_narration: Push a particle with a steady force forever, and Newton promises it just keeps speeding up, faster and faster, with no ceiling at all. But nature has hung a wall in the sky, the speed of light, and nothing made of matter ever gets through it.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:light-wall>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_4:gamma_runaway>> Push a particle with a steady force forever, and Newton promises it just keeps speeding up, faster and faster, with no ceiling at all. But nature has hung a wall in the sky, the speed of light, and nothing made of matter ever gets through it.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Dynamics at large velocity|id=sec-1>>So something in the old rule must bend. The rule we are bending is the one you have trusted for years, force equals mass times acceleration.
segments.text_with_markers: <<SECTION:Dynamics at large velocity|id=sec-1>>So something in the old rule must bend. The rule we are bending is the one you have trusted for years, force equals mass times acceleration. <<POINT:light-wall>>

segments.raw_narration: Here is the honest question. If a constant force never stops pushing, why does the particle refuse to break the light barrier? Where does all that pushing go?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:speed-axis>> Here is the honest question. If a constant force never stops pushing, why does the particle refuse to break the light barrier? Where does all that pushing go? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: The secret is momentum. In Newton's world momentum is simply mass times velocity, so push harder and it grows without limit, a perfectly straight line climbing forever.
segments.text_with_markers: The secret is momentum. In Newton's world momentum is simply mass times velocity, so push harder and it grows without limit, a perfectly straight line climbing forever. <<TRACE:newton-line>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)|id=text-gamma>>But relativity inserts a new character into the formula, a number we call gamma, equal to one over the square root of one minus the velocity squared over the speed of light squared.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:relativity-curve>> <<WRITE_TEXT:gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)|id=text-gamma>>But relativity inserts a new character into the formula, a number we call gamma, equal to one over the square root of one minus the velocity squared over the speed of light squared. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Relativity inserts a number gamma equal to one over the square root of one minus the velocity squared over the speed of light squared.
segments.text_with_markers: Relativity inserts a number gamma equal to one over the square root of one minus the velocity squared over the speed of light squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}|id=eq-1|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: Now here is the lovely part. At everyday speeds, walking, driving, even rocketing into orbit, v over c is so tiny that gamma is almost exactly one, so the relativistic curve lies right on top of Newton's line.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:agreement-region>> Now here is the lovely part. At everyday speeds, walking, driving, even rocketing into orbit, v over c is so tiny that gamma is almost exactly one, so the relativistic curve lies right on top of Newton's line. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: That overlap is why Newton's law has worked flawlessly for three centuries. In this whole shaded region the two pictures simply agree.
segments.text_with_markers: That overlap is why Newton's law has worked flawlessly for three centuries. In this whole shaded region the two pictures simply agree. <<POINT:agreement-region>>

segments.raw_narration: So the real momentum of a particle is its rest mass times gamma times its velocity. The rest mass is just the ordinary mass you would measure standing still beside it.

segments.raw_narration: And watch what gamma does as the speed creeps toward the speed of light. The bottom of that fraction, the square root, shrinks toward zero, so gamma swells toward infinity, and the momentum shoots straight up.
segments.text_with_markers: And watch what gamma does as the speed creeps toward the speed of light. The bottom of that fraction, the square root, shrinks toward zero, so gamma swells toward infinity, and the momentum shoots straight up. <<TRACE:relativity-curve>>

segments.raw_narration: So now we can answer where the pushing goes. The force keeps adding momentum, but because gamma is exploding, almost all of that momentum goes into making the particle harder to accelerate, not faster.

segments.raw_narration: Here's an example from the chapter. A particle starts at rest at the origin, and a constant force F begins acting on it at time t equals zero. Because the particle starts from rest and the force always points the same way, the motion is along one direction only. We want the speed of the particle at time t. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Particle at rest at origin, constant force F from t=0. Find speed v at time t.|id=ex-q-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: Here's an example from the chapter. A particle starts at rest at the origin, and a constant force F begins acting on it at time t equals zero. Because the particle starts from rest and the force always points the same way, the motion is along one direction only. We want the speed of the particle at time t. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Particle at rest at origin, constant force F from t=0. Find speed v at time t.|id=ex-q-1>>

segments.raw_narration: We start from the equation of motion, which says the rate of change of momentum equals F. That is, d p by d t equals F. <<WRITE_STEP:dp/dt = F|id=ex-step-1-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: We start from the equation of motion, which says the rate of change of momentum equals F. That is, d p by d t equals F. <<WRITE_STEP:dp/dt = F|id=ex-step-1-1>>

segments.raw_narration: The law of motion says force equals the rate of change of this relativistic momentum.
segments.text_with_markers: The law of motion says force equals the rate of change of this relativistic momentum. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt}|id=eq-3|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: Now we integrate both sides. The integral of d p from zero to p equals the integral of F d t from zero to t. Since F is constant, this gives p equals F times t. <<WRITE_STEP:∫₀ᵖ dp = ∫₀ᵗ F dt  →  p = Ft|id=ex-step-1-2>>
segments.text_with_markers: Now we integrate both sides. The integral of d p from zero to p equals the integral of F d t from zero to t. Since F is constant, this gives p equals F times t. <<WRITE_STEP:∫₀ᵖ dp = ∫₀ᵗ F dt  →  p = Ft|id=ex-step-1-2>>

segments.raw_narration: Now we put in the relativistic momentum: p equals m naught times v divided by the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. Setting that equal to F times t gives m naught v over square root of one minus v squared over c squared equals F times t. <<WRITE_STEP:m₀v / √(1 − v²/c²) = Ft|id=ex-step-1-3>>
segments.text_with_markers: Now we put in the relativistic momentum: p equals m naught times v divided by the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. Setting that equal to F times t gives m naught v over square root of one minus v squared over c squared equals F times t. <<WRITE_STEP:m₀v / √(1 − v²/c²) = Ft|id=ex-step-1-3>>

segments.raw_narration: Solving this for v, we find v equals F times t times c divided by the square root of m naught squared c squared plus F squared t squared. Notice that however large t may be, v can never exceed c. No matter how long you apply the force, the speed stays less than the speed of light. <<WRITE_ANSWER:v = Ftc / √(m₀²c² + F²t²),  v < c always|id=ex-ans-1>>

Notice that however large t may be, v can never exceed c. No matter how long you apply the force, the speed stays less than the speed of light. <<WRITE_ANSWER:v = Ftc / √(m₀²c² + F²t²),  v < c always|id=ex-ans-1>>

At everyday speeds, walking, driving, even rocketing into orbit, v over c is so tiny that gamma is almost exactly one, so the relativistic curve lies right on top of Newton's line. <<PAUSE:short>> That overlap is why Newton's law has worked flawlessly for three centuries. In this whole shaded region the two pictures simply agree. <<POINT:agreement-region>> <<FOCUS:relativity-curve>> So the real momentum of a particle is its rest mass times gamma times its velocity. The rest mass is just the ordinary mass you would measure standing still beside it. <<PAUSE:short>> The real momentum of a particle is its rest mass times gamma times its velocity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{p} = m_0\,\gamma\,\vec{v}|id=eq-2|boxed>> And watch what gamma does as the speed creeps toward the speed of light. The bottom of that fraction, the square root, shrinks toward zero, so gamma swells toward infinity, and the momentum shoots straight up. <<TRACE:relativity-curve>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:relativity-curve>> So now we can answer where the pushing goes. The force keeps adding momentum, but because gamma is exploding, almost all of that momentum goes into making the particle harder to accelerate, not faster. Here's an example from the chapter. The bird is hit before the trigger moves. That is the impossible world. <<FOCUS:light-cone-line>> So the speed limit is not a stubborn rule about how engines work. It is nature protecting cause and effect: if effect can never come before its cause in any frame, then c must be the ultimate speed. <<WRITE_KEY:Limit protects cause before effect|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> And this is bigger than bullets and birds. No particle, no message, no influence of any kind can outrun light, because all of them would break this same chain of cause and effect. <<POINT:faster-than-light-signal>> <<PAUSE:short>> Now here is a delicious loophole. Physicists asked: what about particles that are born already faster than light and can never slow below it? They called them tachyons. <<UNFOCUS>> In their hypothetical world effect always precedes cause, and crucially they could never interact with us, so our cause and effect stays safe. Whether tachyons truly exist is still an open question. <<FOCUS:light-cone-line>> So remember this: light's speed, about three hundred thousand kilometers per second, is the universe's ultimate speed limit, and nature enforces it not out of stubbornness but to keep every cause safely ahead of its effect. <<PAUSE:short>>

47.1 THE PRINCIPLE OF RELATIVITY
The principle of relativity is not a new concept for
us. We have seen that all frames of reference that
move with uniform velocities with respect to an inertial
frame are themselves inertial. Newton’s laws of motion
are valid in the same form in all such frames. Standing
on a railway platform, you can drop a stone in such a
way that it hits your left foot. If you repeat the same
experiment in a train moving smoothly with a uniform
velocity, the stone will again strike your left foot. One
cannot distinguish between two inertial frames by
repeating the same experiment in the two frames. No
experiment done inside the train can tell whether the
train is at rest at a platform or is moving at 120 km h
−1
with respect to the platform provided there are no
jerks, the train does not speed up or speed down and
it does not bend.
This is the principle of relativity. There is no
preferred inertial frame. All frames are equivalent.
The motion between two frames is relative—you can
choose any of the frames and call it at rest and the
other in motion.
We can understand this on the basis of Newton’s
laws of motion. These laws have the same form in all
inertial frames. Whether you measure acceleration,
force and mass on the platform or on the train, force
always equals mass times acceleration. As the results
of experiments are governed by Newton’s law, identical
experiments will give identical results irrespective of
the frame involved. But Newton’s laws govern only the
experiments of mechanics ! Can we do an experiment
related to electricity inside a train and tell if the train
is moving or is at rest ?
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about something you've actually felt before, even if you didn't have a name for it. Imagine you're standing on a railway platform and you drop a stone so it lands right on your left foot. Easy enough. Now imagine you climb onto a train that's gliding along smoothly at a steady speed, and you drop the same stone. Where does it land? Right on your left foot again. Nothing changes. That's a surprisingly deep idea.

Here's what's going on. A frame of reference is just a point of view from which you measure motion. An inertial frame is one that's either sitting still or moving at a constant velocity, with no speeding up, no slowing down, no turning. The key insight is this: any frame that moves at a steady velocity relative to an inertial frame is itself an inertial frame, and Newton's laws of motion work exactly the same in all of them. Force always equals mass times acceleration, whether you measure it on the platform or inside the train.

Now think about what that means. If you're sealed inside that smoothly moving train with no windows, and you do experiments dropping stones, rolling balls, pushing carts, there is no experiment in mechanics you can perform that would tell you whether the train is parked at the station or rushing along at a hundred and twenty kilometers per hour. As long as there are no jerks, no speeding up or slowing down, and the train doesn't bend around a curve, everything behaves identically.

This is the principle of relativity. There's no special, preferred frame that we can call the true rest frame. All inertial frames are equally valid. Motion between two frames is relative, which means you're free to pick either one and call it the one at rest, and call the other one moving. Neither choice is more correct.

Why does this work? Because the results of experiments are governed by Newton's laws, and those laws keep the same form in every inertial frame. Identical experiments give identical results no matter which frame you're in. But notice the careful word here: Newton's laws govern only mechanics, things like motion and force. So a natural and very important question hangs in the air. What about electricity? Could an experiment with electricity, done inside the train, finally reveal whether the train is moving or at rest? Hold onto that question, because it's exactly where the story gets interesting.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's start with something strange and wonderful. Maxwell's laws, which describe electricity and magnetism, predict that light travels through empty space at one fixed speed, about three hundred million meters per second, which we call c. Now here's the big question this section asks: do Maxwell's laws look the same to everyone, no matter how they're moving? If they do, then light must travel at that same speed c for every observer, even ones moving at different speeds. And experiments confirm this surprising fact.

To see why this feels so weird, picture two observers, A and B, watching a flash of light called W. At time zero, A, B, and the light pulse are all at the same spot. Then B moves to the right at half the speed of light, while the light pulse races off to the right at full speed c. Each observer writes down distances in a diary. Now think about what we'd normally expect. If A says the light is at a certain distance, and B has moved away from A, then surely the light should be closer to B than to A, because B chased after it a little. In everyday thinking, the distance from A to the light should equal the distance from A to B plus the distance from B to the light.

But that's not what the diaries say. They show that A measures the same distance to the light as B does, even though A and B are clearly separated. That breaks our simple addition rule, and it tells us something deep is wrong with our assumptions.

So what could be off? Maybe one second for A is not the same as one second for B. Or maybe one meter for A isn't the same as one meter for B. In other words, maybe time and length themselves aren't fixed and universal the way we always assumed.

There are only two ways out. Either Maxwell's laws keep the same form in every frame, and we must rethink clocks and rulers. Or Maxwell's laws change form depending on how you move. If the second were true, then electrical and optical experiments inside a moving train could reveal its motion. But the famous Michelson and Morley experiment tried exactly that and failed, beautifully. Motion couldn't be detected. So we accept the first option. Einstein captured this in two postulates: the laws of nature look the same in all inertial frames, and the speed of light in vacuum is the same value c for everyone.

topics.our_understanding:
This section is where relativity gets really surprising, so let's take it slowly. We start with the idea that the postulates of relativity force us to rethink length and time. Imagine two identical metre sticks and two identical clocks. Put one of each on a railway platform and the other on a moving train. They behave differently, and we're going to figure out exactly how.

First, picture a rod moving sideways, perpendicular to its length. We do a clever paint experiment with two equal rods, one painted red and one painted blue, sliding one over the other. If the moving rod shrank, it would leave red marks; if it stretched, blue marks. But here's the trick: by the principle of relativity, either rod can be called the one at rest. The two viewpoints must agree, and the only way they can agree is if the rod's length stays exactly the same when it moves perpendicular to its length. So no change there.

Now comes time dilation. Picture a light pulse bouncing between two mirrors. In the frame where the mirrors sit still, the pulse travels twice the rod length, so the time between bounces is two L over c. But to a moving observer, the mirror has shifted sideways, so the light travels a longer, slanted path. Since light always moves at the same speed c, that longer path means more time. Working through the geometry gives us the famous result: the moving clock's time interval is longer by a factor we call gamma, which is one over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. Gamma is always bigger than one. We call the short time, measured where both events happen at the same place, the proper time. The stretched time is improper. So a moving clock runs slow.

Then we look at a rod moving along its own length. The same light-clock reasoning shows the rod is shorter by a factor of gamma. That's length contraction.

Finally, two beautiful puzzles. Simultaneity depends on your frame: two doors that open together on the ground open at different times for a passing train. And moving clocks are out of synchronization, with the rear clock leading the front one. Notice how every one of these effects ties back to the constant speed of light.

book_examples.verbatim_text: Example 47.1: A person in a train moving at a speed 3 × 10^7 m s^−1 sleeps at 10.00 p.m. by his watch and gets up at 4.00 a.m. How long did he sleep according to the clocks at the stations? Solution: The time interval measured by the watch is the proper time interval because the events, 'sleeping' and 'getting up', are recorded by the single clock (the watch). The clocks at the stations represent the ground frame and in this frame he sleeps at one place and gets up at another place. Thus, the time interval measured by the station clocks is improper time interval and is more than the proper time interval. The duration of his sleep in the ground frame is ∆t′ = γ∆t = ∆t / √(1 − v²/c²) = 6 h / √(1 − (3 × 10^7 / 3 × 10^8)²) = 6 h √(100/99) = 6 hours 1.8 minutes.
book_examples.lesson_focus: The time measured on the single moving watch is proper time, and the ground clocks measure a slightly longer improper time due to time dilation.
setup_facts: train speed = 3 × 10^7 meters per second
speed of light c = 3 × 10^8 meters per second
ratio v over c = one tenth
sleep duration on the watch = 6 hours (10 p.m. to 4 a.m.)
watch reading is the proper time interval
station clocks give improper time interval
gamma factor gives √(100/99)
answer = 6 hours and 1.8 minutes

book_examples.verbatim_text: Example 47.2: The passenger of example 47.1 slept with his head towards the engine and feet towards the guard's coach. If he measured 6 ft in the train frame, how tall is he in the ground frame? Solution: In the ground frame, the passenger is moving with a velocity c/10. His length is thus contracted. The length measured in the train frame is the rest length of the passenger as the passenger is at rest in the train. Thus, his length in the ground frame is L′ = 6 ft √(1 − (1/10)²) = 6 ft √(99/100) = 5 feet 11.6 inches.
book_examples.lesson_focus: A length measured parallel to the motion is contracted, so the passenger's rest height of six feet appears slightly shorter from the ground.
setup_facts: rest height in train frame = 6 feet
passenger speed in ground frame = c divided by 10
v over c = one tenth
length is measured parallel to the direction of motion
contraction factor = √(99/100)
answer = 5 feet 11.6 inches

book_examples.verbatim_text: Example 47.3: Suppose the rest length of the box in figure (47.6) is 30 light seconds. The train T1 travels at a speed of 0.8c. Find the time elapsed between opening of D1 and D2 in the frame of T1. Solution: The box moves in the frame of T1 with a speed of 0.8c so that γ = 1 / √(1 − (0.8)²) = 1 / 0.6. In this frame, D2 opens after D1. The time elapsed between the openings of the doors is Lv/c² γ = (30 light seconds) × (0.8c) / (c² × 0.6) = (30 s)c × (0.8c) / (c² × 0.6) = 40 s.
book_examples.lesson_focus: Events that are simultaneous in the ground frame are separated in time in a moving frame, and the time gap can be computed using L times v over c squared times gamma.

train T1 speed = 0.8c
v over c = 0.8
gamma = 1 divided by 0.6
30 light seconds equals 30 seconds times c
time gap formula = L times v over c squared times gamma
answer = 40 seconds

Every round trip is one tick. <<TRACE:light-vertical>> <<FOCUS:mirror-top>> <<SECTION:The light clock|id=sec-1>>Sitting still, the pulse just goes straight up to the top mirror and straight back down. Simple, honest, and the time for one tick we will call t-nought. <<POINT:mirror-top>> <<FOCUS:base-vt>> Now here is the interesting thing. Suppose I run past this clock, or what is the same, the clock glides past me to the right at speed v. <<POINT:base-vt>> <<FOCUS:light-diagonal>> While the light travels from the bottom mirror up to the top, the whole clock has moved sideways. So from where I stand, the pulse does not go straight up. It goes along a slanted, diagonal path. <<TRACE:light-diagonal>> <<FOCUS:hyp-ct>> Look closely and you will see a right triangle hiding here. The bottom side is how far the clock moved, v times t. The slanted side is the path the light took, and the upright side is the same mirror gap as before. <<POINT:hyp-ct>> <<FOCUS:hyp-ct>> Now the crucial fact that nature forces on us: the speed of light is the same for everyone. So that long diagonal path was also covered at speed c, which means the slanted side has length c times t. <<POINT:hyp-ct>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:light-diagonal>> Here is the puzzle. The light in the moving clock had a longer road to travel, but it is forbidden from going any faster. So what has to give? <<PAUSE:long>> The slanted light path squared equals the sideways distance squared plus the mirror gap squared, just Pythagoras on the triangle we drew. <<WRITE_EQUATION:(ct)^2 = (vt)^2 + (ct_0)^2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:leg-ct0>> <<WRITE_KEY:Moving clock runs slow by the factor root of one minus v squared over c squared|id=key-1>>Time itself must stretch. And it is not a trick of this clock. Every clock, even your heartbeat, must agree. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:rod-rest>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_3:length_contraction>> <<SECTION:Length contraction|id=sec-2>>Now if time gets squeezed, something else must give too. A person on a train moving at three times ten to the seventh meters per second goes to sleep at ten p.m. by his watch and gets up at four a.m. That's six hours of sleep on his watch. How long per station clocks?|id=ex-q-1>> First, let's identify which time is which. That proper time is six hours. <<WRITE_STEP:Watch reading = proper time, delta t = 6 hours|id=ex-step-1-1>> The station clocks belong to the ground frame, and in that frame he falls asleep at one place and wakes up at another. So the station clocks give the improper time interval, which is longer. The speed v is three times ten to the seventh meters per second, and the speed of light c is three times ten to the eighth meters per second. So v over c is one tenth. topics.our_understanding:
Here's where relativity changes the rules of motion. You've spent years learning Newton's second law, which says force equals mass times acceleration. That law works beautifully for everyday speeds. But when a particle starts moving at speeds close to the speed of light, that simple law no longer tells the whole story. So physicists rewrote the rules, and in this section we just state the corrected versions rather than proving them.

First, let's talk about momentum. In Newton's world, momentum is just mass times velocity. In relativity, the momentum of a particle equals its rest mass times the factor gamma times its velocity. That gamma factor is one divided by the square root of one minus the velocity squared over the speed of light squared. When the speed is small, gamma is almost one, and we get back the old familiar momentum. But as the speed climbs toward the speed of light, gamma grows larger and larger.

Now here's a fascinating idea. We can group rest mass times gamma together and call it the moving mass. This means the mass of a particle actually appears different to different observers, depending on how fast the particle moves relative to them. The mass you measure when you're sitting still right next to the particle is called its rest mass. Someone watching it zoom past would measure a larger moving mass.

The new law of dynamics says that force equals the rate of change of this relativistic momentum over time. Notice this looks like Newton's law in spirit, but now momentum carries that gamma factor inside it. From this, we get conservation of relativistic momentum: if no force acts on a particle, its momentum stays constant.

The most beautiful payoff comes when you imagine pushing a particle with a steady force forever. You'd think it would keep speeding up without limit. But the math shows something profound. No matter how long you push, the speed creeps closer and closer to the speed of light but never reaches it. The speed of light is a cosmic speed limit built right into the structure of motion itself. That single insight is one of the deepest truths in all of physics.

Thus, we can write dp/dt = F, or, integral from 0 to p of dp = integral from 0 to t of F dt, or, p = Ft, or, m0 v over square root of (1 minus v squared over c squared) = Ft. Solving, v = Ftc over square root of (m0 squared c squared plus F squared t squared). Note that however large t may be, v can never exceed c. No matter how long you apply a force, the speed of a particle will be less than the speed c.

topics.our_understanding:
Here's one of the most famous ideas in all of physics: mass and energy are really the same thing. Einstein discovered that any mass m has an energy locked inside it, and that energy equals the mass times the speed of light squared. We write this in words as energy equals m times c squared. Because the speed of light is such a huge number, even a tiny bit of mass holds an enormous amount of energy. This means matter can turn into energy, and energy can turn into matter. They're just two names for the same physical quantity.

Now think about what happens when you push on a particle. You do work on it, so you give it energy. Since energy and mass are the same, giving it energy also increases its mass. When a particle just sits still, its mass is called its rest mass, and the energy bottled up inside it is called its rest mass energy. That rest energy equals the rest mass times c squared.

But what if the particle moves? Then its mass grows. The faster it goes, the bigger its mass becomes, following the relativity rule where you divide the rest mass by the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. So the total energy is this larger mass times c squared.

Here's the beautiful part. If you expand that total energy formula carefully, you find it equals the rest mass energy plus one half times the rest mass times v squared, plus some tiny extra terms. The extra energy beyond the rest energy is what we call kinetic energy. And notice, when the speed v is much smaller than the speed of light, those tiny extra terms vanish, and the kinetic energy becomes one half m v squared, exactly the old familiar formula from ordinary physics. So relativity contains the old physics inside it.

There's also a neat relationship linking energy and momentum. If you combine the formula for momentum and the formula for energy, you get that energy squared equals rest mass squared times c to the fourth, plus momentum squared times c squared. This is powerful because it works even for things with no rest mass at all. Take a photon, a particle of light. Its rest mass is zero, so this rule simplifies to energy equals momentum times the speed of light, or equally, momentum equals energy divided by c. That's why light, even though it has no rest mass, still carries momentum and can push on things.

topics.orig_book_content:
47.6 THE ULTIMATE SPEED
We saw in example (47.4) that even if we continue
to apply a force on a particle for a long time, its speed
cannot exceed c. This is a very general result in special
relativity. In fact, no information can be sent with a
speed greater than c. If we assume that information
can be sent with a speed greater than c, it turns out
that we shall have frames in which a bullet will hit
the bird before it is actually fired, a dog can die before
it is born and so on. If the effect cannot precede its
cause in any frame, then c is the ultimate speed for
any material particle or information.
Scientists have worked out the mathematics for a
world in which all the particles are moving with
respect to each other with speeds greater than c. Such
a world can exist without violating the postulates of
relativity but these particles can never be slowed down
to a speed less than c. The particles of this hypothetical
world cannot interact with ours and in that world,
effect will always precede its cause. Such particles are
named tachyons and a group of physicists is working
to explore the possibility of the actual existence of such
particles. These large speeds and the unworldly results
remind us of several stories from Indian Scriptures
and no wonder the idea of tachyons was mooted by an
Indian scientist E.C.G. Sudarshan.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about one of the most striking ideas in all of physics: there is a cosmic speed limit. We met this earlier when we looked at what happens if you keep pushing on a particle. You might think that if you keep applying a force for long enough, the particle would just go faster and faster without limit. But that's not what happens. No matter how long you push, its speed can never reach the speed of light, which we call c. That's about three hundred thousand kilometers per second. This isn't just a quirk of one experiment, it's a deep, general result of special relativity. And it goes even further: no information of any kind can travel faster than light.

Now why should nature care so much about this limit? The answer is beautiful, and it comes down to cause and effect. Think about what happens if something could travel faster than light. Physicists worked out the math, and they found something absurd. There would be reference frames, perfectly valid ones, in which a bullet hits a bird before the bullet is actually fired. There would be frames where a dog dies before it is even born. The effect would come before the cause. That breaks the most basic rule we trust about how the world works: causes always come first, then their effects. Since we never want the effect to come before its cause in any frame at all, the speed of light must be the ultimate speed for any material particle or for any information.

Here's a fascinating twist, though. Scientists have explored a hypothetical world made of particles that always move faster than light. Surprisingly, such a world doesn't break the rules of relativity, as long as those particles can never slow down below the speed of light. They live entirely on the other side of the speed limit. These imagined particles are called tachyons. In their world, effect would always come before cause, and they could never interact with our world. A group of physicists is still working to see whether tachyons actually exist. And here's a point of pride: the idea of tachyons was first proposed by an Indian scientist named E. C. G. Sudarshan. So the speed of light isn't just a number, it's the boundary that keeps cause and effect in their proper order.
