That is the absurd world we have to rule out. Here is where it comes from. Earlier we kept pushing on a particle, expecting it to go faster and faster forever, but its speed crept toward one wall and never crossed it: the speed of light, c, about three hundred thousand kilometers per second. <<SECTION:The cosmic speed limit|id=sec-1>><<WRITE_KEY:Nothing exceeds c, about 300000 kilometers per second|id=key-1>> <<POINT:light-cone-line>> <<PAUSE:short>> Any speed v of a particle or signal must stay below the speed of light c, which is about three hundred million meters per second. <<WRITE_EQUATION:v < c \approx 3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now you might ask: why should nature care so fiercely about this one number? Why not just let something, anything, go a little bit faster? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:frame-rest>> The answer is about cause and effect. Let me set up two observers. Here is me, at rest, with space across and time going up. <<FOCUS:frame-moving>> And here is a friend gliding past to the right at a steady speed v. Relativity insists the laws of physics look exactly the same for both of us. <<POINT:frame-moving>> Now suppose I fire off a signal that beats light to its target. The cause is here, the effect is over there, and the line between them is almost flat because the signal is so fast. <<WRITE_TEXT:cause then effect, in my frame|id=text-1>> <<TRACE:faster-than-light-signal>> In my frame, fine: cause first, then effect. But watch what my moving friend sees, because in relativity space and time tilt together when you change frames. <<POINT:velocity-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:effect-event>> For a signal faster than light, that tilt is enough to flip the order: my friend sees the effect happen before the cause. The bird is hit before the trigger moves. That is the impossible world. <<FOCUS:light-cone-line>> So the speed limit is not a stubborn rule about how engines work. No particle, no message, no influence of any kind can outrun light, because all of them would break this same chain of cause and effect. <<POINT:faster-than-light-signal>> <<PAUSE:short>> Now here is a delicious loophole. Physicists asked: what about particles that are born already faster than light and can never slow below it? They called them tachyons. <<UNFOCUS>> In their hypothetical world effect always precedes cause, and crucially they could never interact with us, so our cause and effect stays safe. Whether tachyons truly exist is still an open question. <<FOCUS:light-cone-line>> So remember this: light's speed, about three hundred thousand kilometers per second, is the universe's ultimate speed limit, and nature enforces it not out of stubbornness but to keep every cause safely ahead of its effect. <<PAUSE:short>>

47.7 TWIN PARADOX
As the postulates of special relativity lead to
results which contradict ‘common sense’, a number of
interesting paradoxes have been floated. We shall
describe one of the most famous paradoxes of
relativity—the twin paradox. Consider the twins Ram
and Balram living happily on the earth. Ram decides
to make a trip to a distant planet P, which is at rest
with respect to the earth, and come back. He boards
a spaceship S1, going towards the planet with a
uniform velocity. When he reaches the planet, he
jumps from the spaceship S1 to another spaceship S2
which is going towards the earth. When he reaches
the earth, he jumps out and meets his brother Balram.
As Ram returns from his trip and stands next to
Balram, do they have equal age ? Or is Ram younger
than Balram or is he older than Balram ?
To keep the calculations simple, let us assume the
following data:
Distance between the earth and
                  the planet = 8 light-years,
speed of S1 with respect to earth = 0.8c, and
speed of S2 with respect to earth = 0.8c.
When we said that the distance between the earth
and the planet P is 8 light-years, was it clear to you
that this length is the length as measured from the
earth frame ?
First, let us analyse the events from the point of
view of Balram who is on the earth. For him, both the
spaceships move at a speed 0.8c. So,

When Ram is on S1, he is moving and all his clocks
run slower because of time dilation. His heartbeat,
pulse beat, etc., represent clocks in themselves and
they all run slower. Balram calculates that Ram will
take 8 light-year/0.8c = 10 years to reach the planet P.
But during all these 10 years, time is passing slowly
on S1 and the clocks will read only 10 years × 0.6 = 6
years in this period. The number of breaths taken by
Ram corresponds to 6 years only.
Ram jumped into S2 for the return journey. This
spaceship is also moving at 0.8c and for Balram,  time
passes slowly on S2 as well. Although 10 years passed
on the earth during Ram’s return journey, on the
spaceship the journey was clocked at 6 years. Thus,
Ram has aged only 12 years whereas Balram has aged
20 years during this expedition. Ram has become
younger than Balram by 8 years. This difference in
aging is real in the sense that Ram shows lesser signs
of aging like he has lesser white hairs than his brother.
The observation of Balram is quite consistent with
the special theory of relativity. Such experiments are
indeed performed in laboratories with radioactive
particles. Particles are accelerated to large speeds and
are kept at these speeds for quite some time by
magnetic fields. These particles with large speeds have
longer lives than their counterparts kept at rest in the
laboratory.
The paradox arises when we analyse the events
from the point of veiw of Ram. When he is in the
spaceship S1, to him the distance between the earth
and the planet is not 8 light-years. The earth and the
planet P are moving with respect to Ram and hence
he is measuring contracted length. The separation is,
therefore, 8 light-years × 0.6 = 4.8 light-years. As the
planet is approaching Ram at 0.8c, the time taken by
the planet to reach Ram is 4.8 light-year/0.8c = 6 years.
So according to Ram’s clock, he jumped from S1 to S2
6 years after getting into S1. Once he is on S2, the
earth and the planet are again moving with the same
speed 0.8c. Again, the earth is 4.8 light-years from the
planet and is approaching at 0.8c. It takes 6 years for
the earth to reach Ram. Thus, according to Ram’s
clock, he was out for 12 years from the earth, the same
result as Balram had expected.
But how about Ram’s calculation of Balram’s age ?
When Ram is on S1, the earth is going away from him

with a speed 0.8c. Ram will find that the time on the
earth is passing slower by a factor of 0.6 so that
Balram is aging slower than he is. The same is true
when he is on S2. During this period also, Balram is
moving (towards Ram) with a speed 0.8c and hence
time is passing slowly for Balram. As 12 years passes
on Ram’s clock, he calculates that Balram’s clocks have
advanced only by 12 years × 0.6 = 7.2 years in this
period. According to this analysis, Ram should find
that Balram is 12 – 7.2 = 4.8 years younger than him.
This is the paradox. According to Ram, Balram’s
clocks are running slow and according to Balram,
Ram’s clocks are running slow. Each thinks the other
is younger. Where lies the fallacy ?
The fallacy lies in the fact that Ram has changed
frames whereas Balram has stayed in an inertial
frame. Thus, the roles of the twins are not
symmetrical. The ordering of events are different in
different frames and Ram must take that into account
when he changes frames. Suppose Ram gets into  the
spaceship S1 when his clock reads zero. So does
Balram’s clock. What is the reading of the planet’s
clock at this instant ? According to Balram, it is zero
because both the earth and the planet are at rest and
the clocks are synchronized in his frame. But that is
not so in S1. As Ram gets into S1, he may have the
following conversation with the captain of the ship.
Captain: Welcome aboard S1. I saw you on the
earth, coming towards us. Your jump to board this ship
was perfect. Where are you going ?
Ram: Thank you. I am going to the planet P. How
far is it from here and how long will it take for the
planet to come to us ?
Captain: Planet P is 4.8 light-years from us at the
moment. It is coming towards us at a speed of 0.8c so
it will take 4.8 light-years/0.8c = 6 years for the planet
P to reach us.
Ram: Well, the clocks on the earth and the planet
are running a bit slower than ours. I have been taught
that moving clocks run slow by a factor of γ. This factor
is 1/0.6 for these clocks. So they will advance by 6 years
× 0.6 = 3.6 years by the time the planet reaches us.
Captain: Yes, both the clocks will advance by 3.6
years by the time you jump on the planet P.
Ram: The earth-clock was reading t = 0 as we
passed the earth. This means when I jump on the
planet P the clocks on the earth and the planet will
be reading 3.6 years.
Captain: Here you are mistaken. Don’t you
remember that the planet’s clock is not synchronized
with the earth’s clock ? The planet’s clock is at the rear
end, and hence is running 6.4 years ahead of the
earth’s clock. At the instant the earth’s clock was
reading zero, the planet’s clock was reading 6.4 years.
As the planet reaches us, both the clocks will advance
by 3.6 years. So when you jump out of S1, the earth’s
clock will be reading 3.6 years but the planet’s clock
will be reading 10 years.
Ram understands the logic. In the earth’s frame,
the two clocks read zero simultaneously. But in
S1-frame, the event “planet’s clock reading zero”
occurred several years before “earth’s clock reading
zero”. Six years pass in S1 and Ram finds that the
planet P has reached him. He finds another spaceship
S2 which is heading towards the earth. Ram jumps onto
S2. In the process he looks at the planet’s clock and
finds that it is reading 10 years as calculated by him
on S1. On S2, he starts talking to the commander of the
ship.
Commander: Welcome to S2. How long will you be
with us ?
Ram: Thank you. I am going to Earth. Earth is at
present 4.8 light-years from here and is coming
towards us with a speed of 0.8c. So I will be with you
for 6 years. The captain of S1 told me that the earth’s
clock is reading 3.6 years at this moment whereas the
planet’s clock reads 10 years. There is a difference of
6.4 years in the reading because the two clocks are not
synchronized. Also ….
Commander: Sorry for interrupting you, but you
are mistaken. It is true that the earth’s clock and the
planet’s clock are not synchronized as they are moving
past us. Also the difference in the readings of the two
clocks is 6.4 years. But the planet’s clock is at the front
and the earth’s clock is at the rear. It is the earth’s
clock that is leading by 6.4 years. At the moment the
planet’s clock reads 10 years and hence the earth’s
clock must be reading 16.4 years.
Ram: Hmm… you are right. In S1, the earth was
at the front and its clock lagged behind the planet’s
clock. But in S2 it is the other way round. Indeed the
earth’s clock reads 16.4 years whereas the planet’s
clock reads 10 years.
Commander: That’s right. The earth’s clock is
reading 16.4 years at present. It will advance by another
3.6 years during the 6 years you will be with us. So it
will be reading 20 years when the earth reaches you.
We see that the paradox is resolved.

topics.our_understanding:
Let me tell you about one of the most famous puzzles in all of physics: the twin paradox. Imagine two twins, Ram and Balram, living happily on Earth. Ram decides to travel to a distant planet that is at rest with respect to Earth, and then come back. To keep things simple, we say the planet is eight light-years away as measured from Earth, and Ram's spaceships travel at eight tenths the speed of light, both going and coming.

First, let's look at things from Balram's point of view, the twin who stays home. Because Ram is moving so fast, his clocks, his heartbeat, even his breathing, all run slow. This is called time dilation. The slowing factor here works out to six tenths. Balram figures Ram needs ten years to reach the planet, but only six of those years actually pass for Ram. The return trip is the same, another ten years for Balram, another six for Ram. So when they reunite, Ram has aged twelve years and Balram has aged twenty. Ram is younger by eight years, and this is real, with fewer white hairs to prove it.

Now here comes the puzzle. From Ram's point of view, it's Balram who is moving away and whose clock runs slow. By the same logic, Ram calculates that Balram should be younger. Each twin thinks the other is younger! Where's the trick?

The key insight is this: the two twins are not in the same situation. Ram changes frames, he jumps from one spaceship to another, while Balram stays put the whole time in one steady frame. Because of that switch, Ram must account for something subtle: clocks that are synchronized in one frame are not synchronized in another. When Ram is heading out, the planet's clock is running ahead of Earth's. When he jumps to the return ship, suddenly Earth's clock is the one running ahead, by six point four years. That sudden jump in Earth's clock reading, caused by Ram changing frames, is exactly what resolves the paradox. When you carefully follow Ram's calculation including this leap, you find Balram ends up at twenty years, just as expected. The lesson is that the situation isn't symmetric, and that simultaneity itself depends on your frame.

book_examples.verbatim_text: To keep the calculations simple, let us assume the following data: Distance between the earth and the planet = 8 light-years, speed of S1 with respect to earth = 0.8c, and speed of S2 with respect to earth = 0.8c. First, let us analyse the events from the point of view of Balram who is on the earth. For him, both the spaceships move at a speed 0.8c. So, γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) = 1/0.6. Balram calculates that Ram will take 8 light-year/0.8c = 10 years to reach the planet P. But during all these 10 years, time is passing slowly on S1 and the clocks will read only 10 years × 0.6 = 6 years in this period. Ram jumped into S2 for the return journey. Although 10 years passed on the earth during Ram's return journey, on the spaceship the journey was clocked at 6 years. Thus, Ram has aged only 12 years whereas Balram has aged 20 years during this expedition. Ram has become younger than Balram by 8 years.
book_examples.lesson_focus: From the stay-at-home twin's frame, the traveling twin's clocks run slow by the time-dilation factor, so he ages less over the round trip.
setup_facts: distance between earth and planet = 8 light-years measured in earth frame
speed of S1 = 0.8c
speed of S2 = 0.8c
gamma = 1 over 0.6
time to reach planet in earth frame = 8 light-years divided by 0.8c = 10 years
time passing on the spaceship = 10 years times 0.6 = 6 years each way
Ram ages 12 years total, Balram ages 20 years, difference of 8 years

book_examples.verbatim_text: The paradox arises when we analyse the events from the point of veiw of Ram. When he is in the spaceship S1, to him the distance between the earth and the planet is not 8 light-years. The separation is, therefore, 8 light-years × 0.6 = 4.8 light-years. As the planet is approaching Ram at 0.8c, the time taken by the planet to reach Ram is 4.8 light-year/0.8c = 6 years. Once he is on S2, the earth is 4.8 light-years from the planet and is approaching at 0.8c. It takes 6 years for the earth to reach Ram. Thus, according to Ram's clock, he was out for 12 years from the earth, the same result as Balram had expected. As 12 years passes on Ram's clock, he calculates that Balram's clocks have advanced only by 12 years × 0.6 = 7.2 years in this period. According to this analysis, Ram should find that Balram is 12 – 7.2 = 4.8 years younger than him. This is the paradox.
book_examples.lesson_focus: From the traveling twin's frame, lengths are contracted and the stay-at-home twin's clock appears to run slow, which naively makes each twin think the other is younger.
setup_facts: contracted distance for Ram = 8 light-years times 0.6 = 4.8 light-years
planet approaches Ram at 0.8c, time = 4.8 light-years divided by 0.8c = 6 years each leg
Ram's total trip on his clock = 12 years
Ram calculates Balram's clock advanced 12 years times 0.6 = 7.2 years
Ram concludes Balram is 12 minus 7.2 = 4.8 years younger

book_examples.verbatim_text: Captain: Planet P is 4.8 light-years from us at the moment. It is coming towards us at a speed of 0.8c so it will take 4.8 light-years/0.8c = 6 years for the planet P to reach us. Ram: the clocks on the earth and the planet will advance by 6 years × 0.6 = 3.6 years by the time the planet reaches us. Captain: the planet's clock is at the rear end, and hence is running 6.4 years ahead of the earth's clock. At the instant the earth's clock was reading zero, the planet's clock was reading 6.4 years. As the planet reaches us, both the clocks will advance by 3.6 years. So when you jump out of S1, the earth's clock will be reading 3.6 years but the planet's clock will be reading 10 years. On S2, Commander: It is the earth's clock that is leading by 6.4 years. At the moment the planet's clock reads 10 years and hence the earth's clock must be reading 16.4 years. It will advance by another 3.6 years during the 6 years you will be with us. So it will be reading 20 years when the earth reaches you. We see that the paradox is resolved.
book_examples.lesson_focus: The paradox is resolved by recognizing that clocks synchronized in one frame are not synchronized in another, so when the traveler switches frames the distant clock jumps ahead, restoring agreement that he aged less.
setup_facts: contracted distance = 4.8 light-years, planet reaches Ram in 6 years on his clock
earth and planet clocks advance 6 years times 0.6 = 3.6 years during each leg
clocks are out of sync by 6.4 years
in S1 frame the planet's clock leads by 6.4 years (planet at rear)
when leaving S1: earth clock reads 3.6 years, planet clock reads 10 years
in S2 frame the earth's clock leads by 6.4 years
entering S2: planet clock reads 10 years, earth clock reads 16.4 years
earth clock advances 3.6 more years to reach 20 years

events.text: Earth sees outbound 10 years, return 10 years, total 20 years
Ram ages 12 years, Balram ages 20 years
Q: Earth-planet distance = 8 light-years; speed of S1 = 0.8c, speed of S2 = 0.8c. Ram travels out and back. How much do Ram and Balram each age?
Earth-frame time one way = 8 light-years / 0.8c = 10 years
Ship time one way = 10 years x 0.6 = 6 years
Ram total = 6 + 6 = 12 years; Balram total = 10 + 10 = 20 years
Ram ages 12 years, Balram ages 20 years - Ram is younger by 8 years
Q: From Ram's frame, how much younger does he conclude Balram is?
Contracted distance = 8 light-years × 0.6 = 4.8 light-years
Time per leg = 4.8 light-years ÷ 0.8c = 6 years
Total trip on Ram's clock = 6 + 6 = 12 years
Balram's clock = 12 years × 0.6 = 7.2 years
Ram concludes Balram is 12 − 7.2 = 4.8 years younger
Q: Contracted distance 4.8 light-years, planet approaches at 0.8c, reaching Ram in 6 years. Resolve the twin paradox.
Earth & planet clocks advance = 6 years × 0.6 = 3.6 years
In S1: planet clock leads by 6.4 years (planet at rear)
Leaving S1: earth clock = 3.6 years, planet clock = 6.4 + 3.6 = 10 years
Entering S2: earth clock leads by 6.4 years → earth reads 10 + 6.4 = 16.4 years
Earth clock = 16.4 + 3.6 = 20 years — paradox resolved.
only the traveller switches frames

topics.standalone_narration_text: <<FOCUS:earth>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics_feynman:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_7:twin_journey>> Two twins, the same age. One blasts off to a far planet and races back, and when he steps out of the ship he is younger than his brother. Not a trick, not a feeling, genuinely younger. <<SECTION:The set-up|id=sec-1>>Here is Earth, and way over here is a distant planet sitting still, eight light-years away. Balram stays home; Ram takes the trip. <<POINT:planet>> <<POINT:planet>> Ram rides one ship out at eight tenths the speed of light, and at the planet he leaps onto a second ship heading straight back, again at eight tenths the speed of light. <<TRACE:outbound-path>> <<TRACE:outbound-path>> <<FOCUS:ram-clock>> Now here is the strange thing we learned earlier: when something moves that fast, its clocks run slow. Ram's watch, his heartbeat, even his breathing, all slow down. <<PAUSE:short>> The amount a moving clock slows down is captured by one number, called the time-dilation factor, gamma. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> How slow? We package the slowdown into one number called gamma, the time-dilation factor. At eight tenths of light speed it works out to exactly six tenths. <<FOCUS:balram-clock>> Let's count from Balram's chair on Earth. For him, the planet is eight light-years away and Ram crawls there at eight tenths light speed, so the trip out takes ten years. <<TRACE:balram-clock>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<WRITE_STEP:Earth sees outbound 10 years, return 10 years, total 20 years|id=step-1>>The return is another ten years. So Balram waits twenty whole years for his brother to come home. <<TRACE:return-path>> The time that passes for the travelling twin equals the time on Earth multiplied by the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:t_{\text{Ram}} = t_{\text{Balram}} \times \sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:ram-clock>> But Ram's clock ran slow the entire flight. Multiply Balram's twenty years by six tenths, and only twelve years passed for Ram. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:ram-clock>> <<WRITE_KEY:Ram ages 12 years, Balram ages 20 years|id=key-1>>So when Ram climbs out, he has aged twelve years while Balram has aged twenty. Ram really is eight years younger. <<SECTION:Where is the paradox?|id=sec-2>>Now, you should be itching to object. Motion is relative! From Ram's seat, it is Balram and the whole Earth that flew away and came back. Shouldn't Balram be the younger one? <<POINT:balram-clock>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:turnaround>> Here is the resolution. Look at the trip: only Ram turns around at the planet. He jumps ships, he reverses, he switches from one moving frame to another. Balram never does anything but sit still. Here's an example from the chapter, the twin paradox worked out with simple numbers. The distance between the earth and the planet is eight light-years, measured in the earth frame. Ram's outgoing spaceship S one moves at zero point eight c, and his return spaceship S two also moves at zero point eight c. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Earth-planet distance = 8 light-years; speed of S1 = 0.8c, speed of S2 = 0.8c. Ram travels out and back. How much do Ram and Balram each age?|id=ex-q-1>> Let's analyse everything from the point of view of Balram, who stays on the earth. For him both spaceships move at zero point eight c, so the time-dilation factor gamma is one over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared, which works out to one over zero point six. <<WRITE_STEP:gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = 1 / 0.6|id=ex-step-1-1>> Balram first calculates how long the outward trip takes in his own earth frame. That's the distance, eight light-years, divided by the speed, zero point eight c, which gives ten years. <<WRITE_STEP:Earth-frame time one way = 8 light-years / 0.8c = 10 years|id=ex-step-1-2>> But during all those ten years, time runs slowly on the moving spaceship S one. The ship's clocks read only ten years times zero point six, which is six years for the outbound leg. <<WRITE_STEP:Ship time one way = 10 years x 0.6 = 6 years|id=ex-step-1-3>> Then Ram jumps into S two for the return journey. Again ten years pass on the earth, but on the spaceship that leg is clocked at only six years. So Ram's total is six plus six, twelve years, while Balram lives through ten plus ten, twenty years. <<WRITE_STEP:Ram total = 6 + 6 = 12 years; Balram total = 10 + 10 = 20 years|id=ex-step-1-4>> And so the answer is that Ram has aged only twelve years while Balram has aged twenty years, making Ram younger than Balram by eight years. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Ram ages 12 years, Balram ages 20 years - Ram is younger by 8 years|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter on the twin paradox. Let's analyze the journey from the traveling twin Ram's point of view. From Ram's frame, the distance between earth and the planet is not the full eight light-years that Balram measures. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: From Ram's frame, how much younger does he conclude Balram is?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by contracting the distance. To Ram, the separation shrinks by a factor of zero point six, so the contracted distance is eight light-years times zero point six, which equals four point eight light-years. <<WRITE_STEP:Contracted distance = 8 light-years × 0.6 = 4.8 light-years|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now, the planet is approaching Ram at zero point eight c. So the time taken for the planet to reach him is four point eight light-years divided by zero point eight c, which gives six years for that leg. <<WRITE_STEP:Time per leg = 4.8 light-years ÷ 0.8c = 6 years|id=ex-step-1-2>> On the return leg, the earth is again four point eight light-years away approaching at zero point eight c, taking another six years. So according to Ram's clock, his total trip was twelve years. <<WRITE_STEP:Total trip on Ram's clock = 6 + 6 = 12 years|id=ex-step-1-3>> Here's where the paradox bites. As twelve years pass on Ram's clock, he calculates that Balram's clock advanced only twelve years times zero point six, which is seven point two years. <<WRITE_STEP:Balram's clock = 12 years × 0.6 = 7.2 years|id=ex-step-1-4>> So from Ram's analysis, Balram should be twelve minus seven point two, which is four point eight years younger than him. Each twin thinks the other is younger, and that is the paradox. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Ram concludes Balram is 12 − 7.2 = 4.8 years younger|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter that resolves the twin paradox. The captain tells Ram: planet P is four point eight light-years away, contracted in our frame, and it's coming towards us at zero point eight c, so it will take six years on his clock for the planet to reach us. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Contracted distance 4.8 light-years, planet approaches at 0.8c, reaching Ram in 6 years. Resolve the twin paradox.|id=ex-q-1>> Ram works out the first piece. The clocks on the earth and on the planet will advance by six years times zero point six, which is three point six years, by the time the planet reaches us. <<WRITE_STEP:Earth & planet clocks advance = 6 years × 0.6 = 3.6 years|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now the captain explains the synchronization. In Ram's frame S one, the planet's clock is at the rear end, so it's running six point four years ahead of the earth's clock. When the earth's clock read zero, the planet's clock already read six point four years. <<WRITE_STEP:In S1: planet clock leads by 6.4 years (planet at rear)|id=ex-step-1-2>> As the planet reaches us, both clocks advance by those three point six years. So when you jump out of frame S one, the earth's clock reads three point six years, but the planet's clock reads ten years. <<WRITE_STEP:Leaving S1: earth clock = 3.6 years, planet clock = 6.4 + 3.6 = 10 years|id=ex-step-1-3>> Now you board frame S two, and the commander explains the flip. In this frame it is the earth's clock that leads by six point four years. The planet's clock reads ten years, so the earth's clock must read sixteen point four years. <<WRITE_STEP:Entering S2: earth clock leads by 6.4 years → earth reads 10 + 6.4 = 16.4 years|id=ex-step-1-4>> During the six years you spend on S two heading back, the earth's clock advances another three point six years, reaching twenty years. The traveler aged less, and the paradox is resolved. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Earth clock = 16.4 + 3.6 = 20 years — paradox resolved.|id=ex-ans-1>> <<FOCUS:turnaround>> <<WRITE_TEXT:only the traveller switches frames|id=text-1>>That turnaround makes the twins genuinely different. They are not interchangeable, so there is no contradiction, only an honest answer. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:ram-clock>> So the rule stands: the moving clock runs slow, and because only Ram did the travelling and the turning, Ram is the one who comes home young. <<PAUSE:short>>

questions.q_text: You drop a stone while standing inside a train moving at a constant 120 kilometers per hour in a straight line. Where does the stone land?
options: A. Behind your foot, because the train moves forward while it falls
B. Right on your foot, just as it would if the train were parked
C. Ahead of your foot, because the stone keeps the train's speed
D. It depends on how fast the train is going

questions.q_text: Which of the following is NOT an inertial frame of reference?
options: A. A train parked at a station
B. A train gliding at a steady speed in a straight line
C. A train slowing down as it approaches a station
D. A laboratory sitting still on the ground

questions.q_text: According to the principle of relativity, which statement is correct about inertial frames?
options: A. There is one true rest frame that all motion is measured against
B. The fastest-moving frame is the preferred frame
C. All inertial frames are equally valid and none is the true rest frame
D. Only frames at rest obey Newton's laws

questions.q_text: The principle of relativity, as discussed here, is stated specifically for which kind of physical laws?
options: A. The laws of electricity
B. Newton's laws of mechanics
C. The laws of chemistry
D. The laws of optics

questions.q_text: You are sealed inside a windowless train. You are allowed to do any mechanics experiment you like: dropping stones, rolling balls, pushing carts. Can you determine from these experiments whether the train is parked at the station or moving at a constant 100 kilometers per hour in a straight line? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: No, you cannot tell. Here is the reasoning step by step. First, a train moving at a constant velocity in a straight line, with no speeding up, slowing down, or turning, is an inertial frame, just like a parked train. Second, Newton's laws of motion take exactly the same form in every inertial frame—force equals mass times acceleration in both. Third, since all mechanics experiments are governed by Newton's laws, and those laws are identical in both frames, identical experiments give identical results. A dropped stone lands on your foot, a rolled ball behaves the same, and so on, in both cases. Therefore there is no mechanics experiment that distinguishes the two situations. This is exactly the principle of relativity: motion between inertial frames is relative, and no frame can be singled out as the 'true' rest frame using mechanics alone.

questions.q_text: According to Maxwell's laws and Einstein's postulates, what does every observer measure for the speed of light in a vacuum, regardless of how they are moving?
options: A. A speed that depends on the observer's own speed
B. The same fixed value c for everyone
C. A speed that increases when the observer chases the light
D. A speed that decreases when the observer moves away from the source

questions.q_text: In the thought experiment with observers A and B, the everyday rule that the distance from A to the light equals the distance from A to B plus the distance from B to the light turns out to be false. What does this failure tell us must be reconsidered?
options: A. Maxwell's laws are simply wrong
B. The light was never actually moving
C. Our assumptions that time and length are fixed and universal
D. The observers must have made measurement errors

questions.q_text: What was the significance of the Michelson and Morley experiment in this discussion?
options: A. It proved light travels faster inside a moving train
B. It failed to detect any motion through optical experiments, supporting the idea that Maxwell's laws keep the same form in every frame
C. It showed Maxwell's laws change form when you move
D. It measured the exact speed of the Earth through space

questions.q_text: The section says there are only two logical possibilities. Which pair correctly states them?
options: A. Either light has no fixed speed, or time is absolute
B. Either Maxwell's laws keep the same form in every frame and we rethink clocks and rulers, or Maxwell's laws change form depending on motion
C. Either light is a wave, or light is a particle
D. Either A and B are at rest, or they are moving

questions.q_text: At time zero, observers A and B and a light pulse W start at the same spot. B moves right at half the speed of light, while the pulse moves right at full speed c. Using everyday (Galilean) reasoning, predict how the distance from A to the pulse should compare to the distance from B to the pulse. Then explain what the diaries actually show and why this is a problem.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Everyday prediction: In ordinary thinking, distances simply add. The distance from A to the pulse should equal the distance from A to B plus the distance from B to the pulse. Since B has chased after the light a little (moving right at half c), B should be closer to the pulse than A is. So we'd expect A's measured distance to the light to be larger than B's measured distance.

Step 2 — What the diaries actually record: The measurements show that A measures the same distance to the light as B does, even though A and B are clearly separated from each other.

Step 3 — Why this is a problem: If both observers find the same distance to the light yet are at different positions, the simple addition rule (A-to-light = A-to-B + B-to-light) is violated. This means our hidden assumptions are wrong.

Step 4 — The resolution: The only way both observers can measure light at speed c and get consistent results is if their seconds and their meters are not the same — that is, time intervals and lengths are not absolute. This is exactly the conclusion that leads to special relativity: Maxwell's laws keep their form in every inertial frame, and we must abandon the idea of universal time and length.

questions.q_text: According to the paint experiment with two rods sliding over one another, what happens to the length of a rod that moves perpendicular to its own length?
options: A. It contracts by a factor of gamma
B. It stretches by a factor of gamma
C. It stays exactly the same
D. It depends on how fast the rod moves

questions.q_text: Which of the following correctly describes 'proper time' as discussed in the light-clock argument?
options: A. The longer time measured by a moving observer
B. The short time measured where both events happen at the same place
C. The time measured only by a clock at the centre of the universe
D. The average of the moving and stationary clock readings

questions.q_text: A spaceship moves past Earth at a speed equal to 0.6 times the speed of light. Calculate the gamma factor, and find how long a 10-second interval on the ship's clock appears to last when measured from Earth.
questions.answer: Step 1: Gamma equals one over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. Here v over c is 0.6, so v squared over c squared is 0.36. Step 2: One minus 0.36 equals 0.64. Step 3: The square root of 0.64 is 0.8. Step 4: Gamma equals one divided by 0.8, which is 1.25. Step 5: The moving clock runs slow, so a 10-second interval measured on the ship (the proper time) appears stretched by gamma when seen from Earth: 10 seconds times 1.25 equals 12.5 seconds. So Earth observers see the interval last 12.5 seconds.

questions.q_text: In the light-clock argument, why does the moving observer conclude that more time has passed between bounces than the stationary observer does?
options: A. Because the light slows down when the clock moves
B. Because the light travels a longer slanted path but still moves at the fixed speed c
C. Because the mirrors get farther apart when moving
D. Because the moving observer's eyes react more slowly

questions.q_text: For a train moving along a track, what does relativity say about a pair of clocks placed at the front and rear of the train, as seen from the ground?
options: A. They remain perfectly synchronized in every frame
B. The front clock leads the rear clock
C. The rear clock leads the front clock
D. Both clocks stop running entirely

questions.q_text: For a particle moving at everyday speeds much smaller than the speed of light, what value does the gamma factor take, and what does this mean for relativistic momentum?
options: A. Gamma becomes very large, so momentum is much greater than the Newtonian value
B. Gamma is approximately one, so relativistic momentum reduces to the familiar mass times velocity
C. Gamma becomes zero, so momentum vanishes
D. Gamma equals the speed of light, so momentum is undefined

questions.q_text: An observer sits at rest right next to a particle, while a second observer watches that same particle zoom past at high speed. What can we say about the masses they measure?
options: A. Both measure exactly the same mass since mass is absolute
B. The observer next to the particle measures a larger mass than the one watching it move
C. The observer watching it zoom past measures a larger moving mass than the rest mass measured alongside it
D. The watching observer measures zero mass because the particle is moving

questions.q_text: Suppose you apply a steady, constant force to a particle for an indefinitely long time. According to relativistic dynamics, what happens to its speed?
options: A. It increases without limit and eventually exceeds the speed of light
B. It reaches exactly the speed of light after a finite time and then stops increasing
C. It approaches the speed of light ever more closely but never actually reaches it
D. It increases steadily forever just as Newton's law predicts

questions.q_text: In relativistic dynamics, how is force defined, and how does this differ from the everyday Newtonian picture?
options: A. Force equals rest mass times acceleration, exactly as Newton stated
B. Force equals the rate of change of relativistic momentum, which now carries the gamma factor inside it
C. Force equals gamma times the speed of light
D. Force is always zero for a moving particle

questions.q_text: A student argues: 'If I apply a constant force to a particle forever, then since force equals mass times acceleration, the particle has constant acceleration and its speed must eventually exceed the speed of light.' Explain what is wrong with this reasoning using relativistic dynamics.
questions.answer: Step 1: The student is using Newton's law, force equals rest mass times acceleration, which assumes mass stays fixed. This only works at everyday speeds. Step 2: In relativity the correct law is that force equals the rate of change of relativistic momentum, where momentum is rest mass times gamma times velocity. The gamma factor is one divided by the square root of one minus velocity squared over the speed of light squared. Step 3: As the speed grows toward the speed of light, gamma grows larger and larger without bound. This means that for a fixed force, the same push produces less and less change in velocity, because the momentum is increasingly carried by the growing gamma factor rather than by an increase in speed. Step 4: Effectively the particle behaves as though it has an ever-increasing moving mass, so it resists further acceleration more and more strongly. Step 5: The result is that the speed only creeps closer and closer to the speed of light but never reaches or exceeds it. So the student's conclusion is wrong because the assumption of constant acceleration does not hold; the speed of light is a built-in cosmic speed limit.

questions.q_text: What does Einstein's relation that energy equals mass times the speed of light squared tell us about mass and energy?
options: A. They are two different quantities that can never affect each other
B. They are really the same physical quantity and can convert into one another
C. Mass can become energy but energy can never become mass
D. Only moving objects have energy, while resting objects have only mass

questions.q_text: According to relativity, what happens to a particle's mass as it moves faster and faster?
options: A. Its mass stays exactly equal to its rest mass
B. Its mass decreases toward zero
C. Its mass increases, growing larger as its speed grows
D. Its mass only changes if it has no rest mass

questions.q_text: When a particle moves much slower than the speed of light, what does the relativistic kinetic energy reduce to?
options: A. The rest mass times the speed of light squared
B. One half times the mass times the velocity squared
C. Momentum times the speed of light
D. Zero, because slow particles have no kinetic energy

questions.q_text: A photon has no rest mass. Using the energy-momentum relationship, how is a photon's momentum related to its energy?
options: A. Its momentum equals its energy times the speed of light
B. Its momentum equals its energy divided by the speed of light
C. Its momentum is zero because it has no rest mass
D. Its momentum equals its energy divided by the speed of light squared

questions.q_text: An electron has a rest mass of about 9.1 times ten to the power minus 31 kilograms. Using the idea that rest energy equals rest mass times the speed of light squared, estimate the rest mass energy of the electron. Take the speed of light to be 3 times ten to the power 8 meters per second.
questions.answer: Step 1: Write the formula. Rest energy equals rest mass times the speed of light squared. Step 2: Square the speed of light. Three times ten to the power 8, squared, equals nine times ten to the power 16 (in units of meters squared per second squared). Step 3: Multiply by the rest mass. Energy equals (9.1 times ten to the minus 31) times (9 times ten to the 16). Multiply the numbers in front: 9.1 times 9 equals about 81.9. Add the powers of ten: minus 31 plus 16 equals minus 15. Step 4: Combine. Energy is about 81.9 times ten to the power minus 15 joules, which we rewrite as roughly 8.2 times ten to the power minus 14 joules. So an electron at rest carries about 8 times ten to the minus 14 joules of energy locked in its mass.

questions.q_text: According to the deepest reasoning given, why must the speed of light be the ultimate speed limit for material particles and information?
options: A. Because particles run out of energy before reaching it
B. Because allowing faster speeds would let effects happen before their causes in some valid reference frames
C. Because light is the brightest thing in the universe
D. Because no instrument can measure speeds higher than light

questions.q_text: What is the defining condition that lets hypothetical tachyons exist without violating special relativity?
options: A. They must always move slower than light
B. They must be able to speed up and slow down freely across the speed of light

D. They must remain perfectly at rest

questions.q_text: Who is credited with first proposing the idea of tachyons?

questions.q_text: If you keep applying a force to a particle for an extremely long time, what does relativity predict about its speed?
options: A. It will eventually exceed the speed of light

questions.q_text: Explain, in your own reasoning, why a faster-than-light signal would create a problem with cause and effect, using the examples mentioned in the text.
questions.answer: Step 1: In relativity, different observers (reference frames) can disagree about the timing and order of events that are far apart. Step 2: If a signal or object could travel faster than light, then in some perfectly valid reference frames the order of two connected events could be reversed. Step 3: This means the effect could be observed before its cause. The text gives vivid examples: a frame in which a bullet hits a bird before the bullet is fired, or a frame in which a dog dies before it is born. Step 4: This violates the fundamental principle that a cause must always precede its effect in every frame. Step 5: To preserve causality in all reference frames, no material particle or information can travel faster than light. Therefore the speed of light c is the ultimate speed limit — it is the boundary that keeps cause and effect in their proper order.

questions.q_text: After Ram travels to the distant planet and returns to Earth, which twin has aged less, and by how much?
options: A. Balram has aged less, by eight years
B. Ram has aged less, by eight years
C. They have aged the same amount
D. Ram has aged less, by twenty years

questions.q_text: What is the essential reason the situation between the two twins is not symmetric?
options: A. Balram moves faster than Ram during the trip
B. Ram changes reference frames when he turns around, while Balram stays in one steady frame
C. The planet is moving relative to both twins
D. Time dilation only applies to twins who stay on Earth

questions.q_text: According to the resolution of the paradox, what happens to Ram's reading of Earth's clock at the moment he switches from the outgoing ship to the returning ship?
options: A. Earth's clock appears to stop completely
B. Earth's clock suddenly jumps ahead by six point four years
C. Earth's clock runs backward by ten years
D. Earth's clock stays exactly synchronized with Ram's clock

questions.q_text: Using Balram's frame, the planet is eight light-years away and Ram travels at eight tenths the speed of light. How long does Balram measure for the one-way outbound trip, and how much time passes for Ram on that leg?
questions.answer: Step 1: In Balram's frame, distance is eight light-years and speed is zero point eight light-years per year. Time for Balram equals distance divided by speed, which is eight divided by zero point eight, giving ten years. Step 2: Ram's clock runs slow by the slowing factor of six tenths. So the time elapsed for Ram is zero point six times ten, which equals six years. Therefore Balram measures ten years for the outbound trip while only six years pass for Ram.

questions.q_text: Combine the outbound and return trips to find the total aging of each twin when they reunite. Confirm the eight-year difference.
questions.answer: Step 1: The outbound leg takes ten years for Balram and six years for Ram. Step 2: The return leg is symmetric in distance and speed, so it also takes ten years for Balram and six years for Ram. Step 3: Total for Balram is ten plus ten, which equals twenty years. Total for Ram is six plus six, which equals twelve years. Step 4: The difference is twenty minus twelve, which equals eight years. So Ram has aged eight years less than Balram, confirming the result.

questions.q_text: What deeper principle does the twin paradox ultimately illustrate about events in special relativity?
options: A. The speed of light depends on the observer's motion
B. Whether two clocks are synchronized depends on the reference frame
C. Time dilation never actually occurs in reality
D. Acceleration has no effect on the passage of time
